The Indus cities were never planned. They just grew, like any other old town.
Lothal had the oldest dockyard in the world, and that is settled fact.

There is no reason for sixty minutes in an hour. It is arbitrary, and nobody knows where it came from.
Mesopotamia and the Indus were one civilisation under two names.

plaques.claim: The Ramayana is a news report. Every detail in it has been confirmed by archaeology.
There is only one Ramayana. All the others are corruptions of it.
The story never left India. It is a local tale with no wider life.

The bridge in the Ramayana is just an invention. It tells us nothing worth knowing.
Ravana’s Lanka was a real city, found and mapped, exactly where the poem says.

The epic is a simple story of heroes and villains. It never questions its own side.

Akbar’s tolerance proves that Mughal rule was always tolerant.
Haldighati was a clear and total victory for one side.
Hill forts were held by courage alone. Water and stone had little to do with it.
Ahilyabai Holkar was only a figurehead. The real work was done by the men around the throne, and almost nothing of Ahilyabai’s own survives.

codex.title: A City Laid Out on a Grid
body: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi share a plan: a raised western mound (usually called the citadel) with large public structures, and a bigger lower town of houses on a grid of streets meeting at right angles. Main streets run roughly north-south and east-west; minor lanes branch off them.

Nothing about that is accidental. Grids have to be surveyed before anything is built, which means a decision was taken, enforced and maintained across centuries and across cities more than 500 km apart. We have no palace, no obvious temple and no royal tomb to explain who took that decision — which is one of the most interesting gaps in world archaeology.

codex.title: The Great Bath
body: On the citadel at Mohenjo-daro sits a sunken tank about 12 m by 7 m and 2.4 m deep, with brick steps at both ends. The floor and walls are of finely fitted sawn brick, sealed with a layer of bitumen — waterproofing, and the earliest large-scale example of it we have in South Asia. A drain carried water out; a nearby well supplied it.

What it was *for* is inference, not evidence. The scale, the location on the citadel and the care taken over waterproofing suggest collective rather than private use, and many archaeologists reach for ritual bathing by analogy with later South Asian practice. That analogy is reasonable and unproven; the bitumen is the fact.

codex.title: Drains Before Palaces
body: Harappan houses have bathing platforms with sloped floors draining to the street. Waste water ran into covered channels of brick running under the lanes, with removable slabs for cleaning and soak-pits to settle solids. The channels have a deliberate gradient, and larger corbelled sewers carry the flow away from the dense quarters.

This is the detail that most surprises people: a Bronze Age civilisation spent its best engineering on sanitation rather than on monuments to rulers. No contemporary city in Mesopotamia or Egypt matches the systematic coverage of Harappan drainage, and nothing in the subcontinent matches it again for roughly two thousand years.

codex.title: The Cubical Weights
body: Harappan weights are small cubes, usually of chert, finished to a high accuracy. They follow a fixed series: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 and then decimal multiples of 160. The unit (ratio 1) is about 0.856 g; the common ratio-16 weight is about 13.7 g.

The same series turns up at Harappa in Punjab, Mohenjo-daro in Sindh, Lothal in Gujarat and Dholavira in Kutch — and Harappan weights have been found in the Gulf. A shared standard over that distance implies something enforcing it: inspection, convention, or both. Standardised measurement is one of the clearest signatures of a complex state, and here it survives while the state itself stays invisible.

codex.title: The Script We Cannot Read
body: About 4,000 inscribed objects survive, using roughly 400–700 distinct signs depending on how you count variants. The average inscription is about five signs long; the longest known is seventeen. Writing usually runs right to left, and some longer texts appear to be boustrophedon — alternating direction line by line.

Decipherment has failed for three structural reasons, not for lack of effort. There is no bilingual text — no Rosetta Stone, no Behistun. The inscriptions are far too short to give the statistical grip that longer texts provide. And we do not know what language was being written, so there is nothing to test a reading against. Claims of decipherment appear regularly; none has been independently verified. Even whether it encodes a full language, or is a non-linguistic system of marks, is genuinely argued.

codex.title: Seals and What They Show
body: Most Indus seals are square steatite tablets, fired to harden and whiten the surface, carved in intaglio with an animal and a short line of signs, and pierced with a boss for a cord. Impressions in clay survive on tags, which tells us they sealed goods and bales.

We can describe the carvings precisely even though we cannot read the signs: a one-horned animal facing a trough or standard (the commonest motif by far), humped zebu bulls, elephants, rhinoceros, tigers, crocodiles, and a few complex scenes such as the seated horned figure often nicknamed "Pashupati". Note the absence of horses and the absence of battle scenes — two silences that historians argue about to this day.

codex.title: Specialists and Workshops
body: Harappan craft was specialised to a degree that implies full-time professionals: long carnelian beads drilled with a hard synthetic-looking stone bit, shell bangles sawn from conch, faience, cast and hammered copper and bronze, standardised fired brick in a 1:2:4 ratio of height to width to length.

The small bronze figure from Mohenjo-daro usually called the "Dancing Girl" was made by lost-wax casting — the same basic technique Chola bronze-casters would use three and a half thousand years later. The chain of craft knowledge in the subcontinent is very long.

codex.title: The Basin at Lothal
body: At Lothal in Gujarat, a trapezoidal basin roughly 215 m by 35 m is lined with burnt brick, with an inlet channel and what appears to be a sluice and spill-way. S. R. Rao, who excavated it, identified it as a tidal dockyard — which would make it among the earliest known anywhere.

Others, including the hydrologist-archaeologist critics who followed, read it as an irrigation or water-storage tank, arguing that the silting and the channel dimensions do not suit seagoing craft. The site also produced a bead factory, a Persian Gulf seal and warehouse platforms, so Lothal was certainly a trading town; what the basin itself did remains unsettled. It is a good example of how a single structure can be solid evidence and contested interpretation at the same time.

codex.title: Meluhha, Dilmun and Magan
body: Mesopotamian cuneiform records name three eastern trading partners: Dilmun (generally identified with Bahrain), Magan (Oman), and Meluhha, further away, which most scholars identify with the Indus region. Texts mention Meluhhan carnelian, ivory, timber and a kind of bird, and even refer to a Meluhhan interpreter living in Mesopotamia.

The archaeology matches: etched carnelian beads, Indus-style weights, and a few Indus seals turn up in Mesopotamia and the Gulf, while Gulf-type seals and Mesopotamian goods appear at Indus sites. There was also an Indus outpost far north at Shortugai in Afghanistan, near the lapis lazuli sources. This was a connected world, moving goods by sea and river across several thousand kilometres.

codex.title: Dholavira: A City Built Around Water
body: Dholavira sits on Khadir Bet, an island in the Rann of Kutch, between two seasonal streams in a landscape with very little rain. Its builders responded by turning the city into a water machine: dams across the streams, channels, and a series of large rock-cut and masonry reservoirs that together occupy a substantial fraction of the walled area.

The city is divided into a citadel, a middle town and a lower town, with a large open ground between them, and it produced a famous signboard of ten large Indus signs. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021. For a region now facing water stress, Dholavira is less a ruin than a case study.

codex.title: Why the Cities Emptied
body: After about 1900 BCE the distinctive Harappan package breaks up: standardised weights and seals go out of use, long-distance trade thins, the big public works stop being maintained, and the large cities shrink. The old story of a violent invasion ending the civilisation is not supported — there is no destruction layer, and the Mohenjo-daro skeletons once read as a massacre turn out to come from different periods and mostly show no battle injuries.

The leading explanations are environmental and systemic. Palaeoclimate records show the summer monsoon weakening from roughly 2200 BCE across a belt from Mesopotamia to north-west India; the Ghaggar-Hakra river system was drying; the Indus shifted channels. Settlement surveys show people moving east and south into many smaller villages rather than disappearing. Separately, migrations into the subcontinent during the second millennium BCE are well supported by linguistics and ancient DNA — but that is a different claim from "an invasion destroyed the cities", and the two should not be confused.

codex.title: The Ziggurat
body: The Great Ziggurat of Ur was built under Ur-Nammu, founder of the Third Dynasty of Ur, as the platform for a temple to the moon god Nanna. Its core is mud brick; its facing is baked brick set in bitumen, pierced by weeper holes so the core could dry. Three monumental staircases converge on the first terrace.

A ziggurat is not a pyramid: it is not a tomb and it is not hollow. It is a solid artificial mountain whose only purpose is to raise a small shrine above the flat delta. The lowest stage still stands because the Neo-Babylonians repaired it, and because the Iraqi restoration of the 1980s rebuilt the façade.

codex.title: Cuneiform: Writing Pressed Into Clay
body: Cuneiform is a writing *technique*, not a language: the same wedge strokes were used to write Sumerian, Akkadian, Elamite, Hittite, Hurrian and Old Persian over three thousand years. A scribe cut a reed stylus to a triangular tip and pressed it into damp clay — pressing is far faster than drawing, and it does not tear the surface.

The system began as pictures and became mixed: some signs stand for whole words (logograms), others for syllables. A trained scribe had to manage several hundred signs with multiple possible readings. Clay is the reason we have so much of it — a discarded tablet survives being buried, and a burnt archive is baked rather than destroyed. Hundreds of thousands of tablets exist, and many remain untranslated simply because there are not enough Assyriologists.

codex.title: What It Takes to Crack a Script
body: Cuneiform fell to a chain of work across half a century. Georg Grotefend guessed at royal names in Old Persian in 1802. Henry Rawlinson copied the Behistun inscription from a cliff face in Iran — the same royal proclamation of Darius I in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Old Persian was simplest and gave the names; the names gave sound values; the sound values opened Akkadian. By 1857 four scholars working independently produced near-identical translations of the same text, which is what settled it.

Three ingredients recur in every successful decipherment: a bilingual or trilingual text, a known language or known proper names to anchor sound values, and a large enough body of text to test hypotheses. Egyptian hieroglyphs had the Rosetta Stone and Coptic. Linear B had Greek underneath it. The Indus script has none of the three — which is why it is still unread, and why it will probably stay unread unless a longer bilingual text is found.

codex.title: Writing Was Invented for Accounting
body: The sequence from Mesopotamia is unusually clear. First, small clay tokens shaped to stand for commodities, sometimes sealed inside clay envelopes as tamper-proof records. Then flat tablets with impressed pictures and separate number signs — recognisable accounts of barley, beer, sheep and labour. Then wedge strokes, then signs used phonetically so that names and grammar could be spelled.

Only after all of that do literary texts appear. The earliest substantial writing anywhere is administrative: who owes what to whom. Writing was not invented to preserve poetry; poetry moved in later and took over the house.

codex.title: Why There Are Sixty Minutes in an Hour
body: Mesopotamian mathematics used a sexagesimal (base-60) place-value system. Sixty is convenient before decimal fractions are easy to write, because it divides exactly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30 — so most everyday fractions come out whole. Sixty shekels made a mina, and sixty minas a talent.

That choice outlived the civilisation that made it. Sixty seconds in a minute, sixty minutes in an hour, 360 degrees in a circle and 60 minutes of arc are all Babylonian inheritances, transmitted through Greek astronomy. Babylonian astronomers also left systematic observational records over centuries — the raw data that later Greek and Indian astronomy built on.

codex.title: Law Carved Where People Can See It
body: Mesopotamia produced the earliest substantial written law collections we have: the laws of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100 BCE), of Lipit-Ishtar, of Eshnunna, and most famously the stele of Hammurabi of Babylon (c. 1754 BCE), now in the Louvre. Hammurabi’s text runs to around 280 provisions on property, family, wages, loans, medical fees and injury.

Two things are worth noticing. The penalties are explicitly graded by the victim’s social rank, so the stele is also a record of inequality. And the point of carving law on a public monument is that the rule is meant to be knowable in advance rather than invented at the moment of judgement — an idea that matters as much as any particular clause.

codex.title: Two Rivers, and the Trouble With Them
body: Sumer sat on the alluvium between the Tigris and Euphrates, in a region with too little rain to farm without irrigation. Canals made the surplus that made the cities; the canals also required collective labour, maintenance schedules and dispute resolution, which is one plausible route from village to state.

The cost arrived slowly. Irrigation in a hot flat basin with a high water table accumulates salt, and texts and crop records show a shift from wheat to the more salt-tolerant barley over centuries, with falling yields in the south. The Indus faced the opposite problem — a monsoon that could fail — and the two civilisations’ different water engineering follows directly from that difference.

codex.title: The Ramayana
body: The Sanskrit Ramayana attributed to Valmiki runs to roughly 24,000 verses in seven books. Its plot is simple enough to summarise in a sentence and has been retold for two thousand years: a prince of Kosala is exiled on the eve of his coronation, his wife is abducted by the king of Lanka, and he recovers her with the help of an alliance.

What the poem is *about* is less simple. It is a sustained examination of obligation — to a parent, a promise, a spouse, a subject, an ally, an enemy — and of what happens when those obligations contradict each other. Scholars date the core to somewhere between the fifth century BCE and the third century CE, composed and reworked over many generations rather than written once.

codex.title: The Seven Books
body: Bala Kanda (childhood and the bow at Mithila), Ayodhya Kanda (the exile), Aranya Kanda (the forest and the abduction), Kishkindha Kanda (the alliance), Sundara Kanda (Hanuman’s journey to Lanka), Yuddha Kanda (the war), Uttara Kanda (afterwards).

Most Sanskritists regard the first and last books as later additions to a core of five. The evidence is internal: differences in language, metre, and in how the characters are treated. That is normal for epic literature everywhere — the Iliad and the Mahabharata show the same layering. Sundara Kanda is frequently recited on its own, which is a clue to how much the tradition values the scout’s journey over the battle.

codex.title: Valmiki and the Shloka
body: Tradition credits the poem to the sage Valmiki, and tells a story about its metre: seeing a hunter shoot a mating bird, Valmiki’s cry of grief came out in a balanced rhythm, and that rhythm became the anustubh shloka — thirty-two syllables in four quarters — in which the epic is composed. The tradition thus roots its own poetry in compassion rather than in craft.

Whether one historical Valmiki wrote the poem is unanswerable and probably the wrong question. What we can say is that the text was transmitted orally by trained reciters long before it was written, which is why it has formulaic repetitions, and why regional recensions differ in thousands of small ways.

codex.title: Many Ramayanas
body: Kamban’s Ramavataram in Tamil (c. 12th century), Molla’s Telugu Ramayanam, Krittibas Ojha’s Bengali version, Madhava Kandali in Assamese, Ezhuthachan in Malayalam, Eknath in Marathi, Tulsidas’s Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi (16th century) — which is the version most north Indian households mean when they say "Ramayana". The Jain Paumacariya of Vimalasuri retells the story with a markedly more dignified Ravana.

The retellings disagree deliberately. Some centre Sita’s suffering and judge Rama for it; some omit the Uttara Kanda entirely; some expand a single episode into an independent work. The scholar A. K. Ramanujan’s essay on this argued that there is no single original with later copies, but a field of tellings in conversation with one another. The useful question about any version is not "is it accurate?" but "what is this teller trying to say?"

codex.title: The Ramayana Outside India
body: Thailand has the Ramakien, painted along the galleries of the royal temple in Bangkok and performed as khon masked dance. Java has the Kakawin Ramayana in Old Javanese, and a wayang shadow-puppet tradition that can run all night. Cambodia has the Reamker, carved at Angkor Wat. Laos has Phra Lak Phra Lam, Malaysia the Hikayat Seri Rama, Myanmar the Yama Zatdaw, and the Philippines the Maranao Maharadia Lawana.

None of this was imposed by conquest. It travelled with traders, monks and scholars across the Bay of Bengal, and each culture localised it — renaming characters, shifting the moral emphasis, absorbing it into local royal ritual. It is one of the clearest examples anywhere of a story becoming shared heritage rather than a cultural export.

codex.title: The Forest as a Place
body: A striking amount of the Ramayana happens outside cities. The vana — forest — is where the exiled live, where sages keep hermitages, and where the people the city does not count have their own societies, alliances and grievances. The epic takes those societies seriously as political actors: the war is won by an alliance, not by Kosala’s army.

Historians of early India read this partly as a memory of the eastward agricultural expansion into the forested Ganga valley during the first millennium BCE: the frontier between settled farming and forest was a real and contested thing, and the literature of the period is full of it.

codex.title: Shabari
body: Shabari is an ascetic woman of the forest who has waited years to offer hospitality, and who tastes each berry first to make sure none is sour before giving them. In most tellings the gesture would be ritually improper and is accepted anyway, explicitly because the intention behind it outranks the form of it.

The episode is small and it is quoted constantly, because the tradition itself uses it to argue that devotion and decency are not the property of the high-born or the learned. Bhakti poets across several centuries and several languages return to her.

codex.title: The Bow in the Epics
body: Epic archery is described as a trained discipline with named weapons, schools and stances. Rama is associated with the bow called Kodanda and with Shiva’s bow Pinaka at Mithila; Arjuna’s bow in the Mahabharata is Gandiva. Dhanurveda, the treatise literature on archery, describes grips, draw lengths, foot positions and the training of the eye.

The archaeology is thinner than the literature, as usual for perishable materials: we have arrowheads of copper, bronze and iron, and depictions in relief sculpture from the Mauryan period onward. Composite bows of horn, wood and sinew are known in the wider region. The epics are better evidence for the *culture* of archery than for its exact technology.

codex.title: The Classical Pharmacy
body: The Charaka Samhita (internal medicine) and Sushruta Samhita (surgery) are the two great classical Indian medical compendia, with the later Ashtanga Hridaya of Vagbhata. Between them they describe hundreds of plant, mineral and animal substances, with methods of preparation and lengthy instructions on identification — because the whole system fails if you misidentify the plant.

The Sushruta Samhita is particularly notable for surgery: cataract couching, the extraction of bladder stones, and a method of nasal reconstruction using a cheek or forehead flap that eighteenth-century British surgeons observed in India and took back to Europe, where it became the basis of modern rhinoplasty. Tulsi, neem, turmeric and ashwagandha all appear in this literature and are all still in common use — which is a reason to study them properly rather than a reason to accept every claim made about them.

codex.title: The Nagara Temple
body: Nagara is the northern Indian temple idiom: a square sanctum (garbhagriha) under a curvilinear tower (shikhara) that rises in a smooth inward curve, topped by a ribbed amalaka disc and a kalasha finial, usually fronted by one or more pillared halls (mandapas) on a raised plinth.

Within Nagara there are strong regional families: the Odishan or Kalinga mode with its near-vertical rekha deul (Lingaraja, Konark), the Khajuraho temples of the Chandelas with their interlocking peaks, the Solanki work at Modhera. Compare Dravida in the south, where the tower is a stepped pyramid of diminishing storeys instead of a curve — the two idioms meet and mix in the Deccan.

codex.title: The Setu in the Epic
body: In the Yuddha Kanda the alliance has to cross from the Indian mainland to Lanka. Valmiki names an engineer, Nala, who directs the work; the army gathers stone and timber and builds a causeway described as a hundred yojanas long and ten wide — epic numbers, meaning "very large".

What is interesting is how procedural the passage is. The sea is first petitioned, then surveyed; the materials are gathered and the work is organised by teams; the crossing takes days. The epic treats a feat of logistics as worth narrating at length, immediately before the fighting it is famous for.

codex.title: Adam’s Bridge: What the Geology Shows
codex.when: Formed over tens to hundreds of thousands of years
body: Between Rameswaram (Pamban Island) in Tamil Nadu and Mannar Island in Sri Lanka runs a chain of shoals, sandbanks and coral reef roughly 48 km long, in water mostly 1–10 m deep. It is shown on charts as Adam’s Bridge and is locally called Rama Setu. Much of it is walkable or waded at low tide; it is not navigable by anything but the smallest craft.

Cores and surveys describe it as a natural formation: a line of old beach ridges, sand spits and coral built up along a shallow ridge during periods of lower sea level, repeatedly reworked by currents and storms. The India–Sri Lanka land connection itself has opened and closed with ice-age sea levels. Dates for the various components run from a few thousand to many tens of thousands of years, and the detail is still being refined — but no survey has produced evidence of construction.
Two statements can both be true: the shoal is a natural feature, and the epic account of a crossing is culturally important. Keeping those claims in separate boxes is the whole skill.

codex.title: Rameswaram and the Shore Shrines
body: The Ramanathaswamy temple at Rameswaram is a major pilgrimage site and one of the twelve Jyotirlinga shrines. The existing structure is largely the work of successive patrons from the twelfth century onward — Pandyas, Setupatis of Ramnad, and later donors — and it contains the longest temple corridor in India, a colonnade of over a thousand carved pillars.

A pattern worth noticing across Indian sacred architecture: the religious association is old, the standing stone is comparatively recent, and the building grew by accretion as patrons added halls, gateways and corridors over centuries. Dating "the temple" as a single object is usually a mistake.

codex.title: Lanka in the Poem
body: Valmiki describes Lanka as a wealthy, well-governed, strongly fortified capital: ramparts and moats, ordered streets, gardens, music, and a court of learned counsellors. Ravana himself is given a formidable education — a scholar of the Vedas, a musician, an astrologer — which is precisely what makes him a tragedy rather than a monster.

That characterisation is deliberate. An epic antagonist who is stupid teaches nothing. The poem’s argument is that learning and power do not immunise anyone against a single ungoverned appetite, and it builds Ravana up carefully so that the point lands.

codex.title: Vibhishana’s Defection
body: Ravana’s brother Vibhishana argues in open court that Sita must be returned, is denounced as a traitor, and leaves to join Rama. His other brother Kumbhakarna also tells Ravana plainly that he is in the wrong — and then fights for him anyway, and dies. The poem places these two responses side by side on purpose.

At the end of the war Rama installs Vibhishana as king of Lanka rather than annexing it. The sequence makes an argument about legitimacy: the war’s stated aim was to right a specific wrong, and the settlement is designed to show that aim was honest. In the Sri Lankan and Southeast Asian retellings Vibhishana is often a considerably more prominent and honoured figure than in north Indian ones.

codex.title: When Duties Collide
body: Both Sanskrit epics are built around collisions between obligations that are each individually right: loyalty to family against justice to a stranger, obedience to a parent against duty to subjects, a vow already sworn against an outcome now visibly wrong. The texts call the resulting difficulty dharmasankata — a crisis of dharma.

Neither epic resolves these by rule. They dramatise the cost of each path and then let the characters choose, and they keep score afterwards. That is why they have survived as teaching texts: a rulebook goes out of date, but a well-constructed dilemma keeps working. The Mahabharata is blunter still, and ends by denying the victors any clean victory at all.

codex.title: Ships of the Indian Ocean
body: For most of recorded history the characteristic Indian Ocean hull was built of planks sewn together with coir rope rather than nailed, caulked with resin and fibre, and rigged with a settee or lateen sail. Sewn hulls flex in a swell and are repairable on a beach with no forge — a serious advantage on long monsoon routes. Teak, from the Western Ghats, was prized and exported for shipbuilding as far as the Gulf.

Evidence comes from a mix of sources: Harappan seal depictions, the first-century Greek merchant handbook Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, Ajanta and Borobudur reliefs, Chola inscriptions, Arab geographers, and excavated wrecks such as the ninth-century Belitung wreck in Indonesian waters. The Periplus names Indian ports and the goods traded from them, which lets us cross-check the archaeology.

codex.title: The Mahabharata
body: Roughly 100,000 shlokas in eighteen books, which makes it about ten times the combined length of the Iliad and the Odyssey and the longest epic poem known. Tradition attributes it to Vyasa. The text itself says it grew: an earlier, shorter work called Jaya, expanded into Bharata, expanded into Mahabharata — the "great" Bharata.

The frame is a succession dispute between cousins that ends in a catastrophic war. Inside that frame the poem carries law, statecraft, cosmology, genealogy, folktales and philosophy, including the Bhagavad Gita. It describes itself as a work in which "whatever is here may be found elsewhere; what is not here is nowhere" — an outrageous claim that it very nearly earns.

codex.title: Who Is Telling You This?
body: The Mahabharata is obsessively layered in narrators. Vyasa composes it; Ganesha is said to write it down; the bard Ugrashravas recites it to sages at a sacrifice; much of the war itself reaches us through Sanjaya, who narrates events to the blind king Dhritarashtra. The Gita comes to the reader as Sanjaya reporting a conversation he did not take part in.

This is not clumsiness. A story told through a chain of narrators keeps reminding you that you are receiving an account, not witnessing an event — and the epic repeatedly exploits that, letting different narrators shade the same episode differently. For a student it is a free lesson in reading sources: always ask who is speaking and what they can actually know.

codex.title: The Bhagavad Gita
body: Eighteen chapters, about 700 verses, set inside the sixth book of the Mahabharata. Arjuna, about to fight his own relatives and teachers, collapses; the dialogue with Krishna that follows is the most widely read philosophical text produced in India.

Its central move is to separate action from attachment to the results of action. You still choose carefully, by your duty and conscience; what you release is the craving and the dread that distort the choosing. "Yoga-sthah kuru karmani" — established in steadiness, do your work. The text offers several routes to that steadiness: karma yoga (action), jnana yoga (knowledge), bhakti yoga (devotion) and dhyana (meditation), and it does not insist that one size fits everyone.

It has been commented on continuously for a thousand years — Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva, Abhinavagupta, and in modern times Tilak, Gandhi and Ambedkar, who read it very differently from one another. Gandhi took it as a text about non-attachment and read the battlefield as allegory; others read it literally. The disagreements are part of the tradition, not a failure of it.

codex.title: Nishkama Karma
body: Nishkama karma means action performed without hunger for its fruit. The verse everyone quotes says: you have a right to the action, never to its fruits; do not be motivated by the fruit, nor attached to inaction.

The common misreading is that this means "do not care what happens". It does not. The text is making a psychological claim: the person who is desperate for a particular outcome chooses worse than the person who is not, because fear and craving distort judgement. A surgeon operating for applause operates worse than one operating for the patient. Equanimity here is an instrument of better action, not an excuse for indifference — and chapter 3 is explicit that refusing to act is itself an action with consequences.

codex.title: The Kurus
body: The Kurus are not only epic characters: they appear in Vedic literature as a real polity in the upper Ganga-Yamuna region, and the later Vedic period there is associated archaeologically with Painted Grey Ware pottery, iron tools, and settled agriculture spreading east through the Ganga plain.

Excavations at Hastinapura in the 1950s under B. B. Lal found a Painted Grey Ware settlement, including evidence of a flood that damaged the site — which is suggestive, since the epic also mentions the capital being abandoned after a flood. "Suggestive" is the correct word. There is no inscription naming an epic character, and no archaeologist can confirm the war. What we can say is that the epic is set in a landscape and a material culture that genuinely existed.

codex.title: Hastinapura and Indraprastha
body: The epic’s two capitals are Hastinapura, the Kuru seat on the Ganga, and Indraprastha, the new city built for the Pandavas — traditionally identified with the area around the Purana Qila in Delhi, where Painted Grey Ware has indeed been found.

Attempts to fix an absolute date for the war have produced a wide spread of answers: traditional Puranic reckoning gives 3102 BCE, astronomical reconstructions from eclipse and planetary references in the text give dates anywhere from the thirty-first to the ninth century BCE, and most academic historians place the *material setting* in the later Vedic period around 1000 BCE while declining to date the events at all. The honest summary is that the question is open, and that the astronomical arguments depend on assuming the verses are precise observational records, which is exactly what is in doubt.

codex.title: How the Epic Fights
body: The Mahabharata’s battles are organised around chariots, elephants, cavalry and infantry, with named formations (vyuhas), heralds, daily rules of engagement and a sunset ceasefire. The chariot is a two-wheeled spoked vehicle with a driver and an archer — fast on flat ground and useless on soft ground, which is why Karna’s stuck wheel is a plausible detail and not just a plot device.

The most important thing about the rules of war in this poem is that almost every turning point involves breaking one: fighting after dark, surrounding a lone boy, striking a man who has laid down his weapon, a mace blow below the waist. The epic notes every violation and never grants the winners a clean victory. After the battle it gives an entire book to the women of both sides mourning, and the surviving Pandavas inherit a depopulated kingdom.

codex.title: The Chakravyuha
body: A vyuha is a battle formation. The chakravyuha is described as a wheel or spiral of concentric layers, each held by named warriors, rotating so that the entry point shifts — easy to enter and designed to be impossible to leave. Its entire defensive logic depends on symmetry: a gap anywhere lets an attacker cut across the layers.

The famous episode is Abhimanyu, sixteen years old, who had learned how to penetrate the formation but not how to withdraw from it. He breaks in, the formation closes, and several of the greatest warriors on the field kill him together — a clear breach of the agreed rules, and the point at which the war stops being a war and becomes a vendetta. It is also the epic’s sharpest comment on partial education.

codex.title: Drona’s Test, and Ekalavya
body: Drona sets a wooden bird in a tree and asks each student what he sees. One sees the tree, the sky, the branch, his brothers, the teacher. Arjuna says he sees only the bird; asked again, only its eye. He is told to shoot. The lesson is about the exclusion of everything irrelevant at the moment of action.

The same teacher provides the epic’s harshest counter-story. Ekalavya, a forest-dwelling prince refused instruction because of his birth, teaches himself from a clay image of Drona and becomes the better archer — and Drona has him give up his bow-thumb, ending his career, to protect Arjuna’s pre-eminence. The epic narrates this without softening it. Read together, the two episodes are a lesson in focus and a lesson in how talent is throttled by social gatekeeping, and the second one is the braver thing for a text to include.

codex.title: The Edicts of Ashoka
body: Ashoka had proclamations cut into rock faces and onto polished sandstone pillars from Afghanistan to Karnataka and from Gujarat to Odisha. They are the oldest substantial Indian texts we can read in the original, on the original stone, dated to a known reign — which makes them the anchor point for early Indian history.

They are not in Sanskrit. They are in Prakrit, the spoken language, written in Brahmi across most of the subcontinent and in Kharosthi in the north-west; at Kandahar there are versions in Greek and Aramaic. An edict is useless if its audience cannot read it, and Ashoka clearly understood that. The pillars are single shafts of Chunar sandstone, up to around 13 m long, with a famously smooth polish, topped by animal capitals.

codex.title: Rock Edict 13: An Emperor’s Remorse
body: Ashoka’s thirteenth Major Rock Edict records the conquest of Kalinga and then does something no other ancient royal inscription does: it gives casualty figures and expresses regret. Around 150,000 deported, about 100,000 killed, and many times that number dead afterwards. The text says the king felt remorse, and that the suffering of the innocent — including the grief of families of every faith — weighed on him.

Historians debate how much of Ashoka’s subsequent policy was genuine conversion and how much was the statecraft of a ruler who had already conquered nearly everything worth conquering. Both readings are defensible. What is not in doubt is the text itself: a victorious emperor chose to have his own regret carved in public, in the language of his subjects, and that choice has no close parallel in the ancient world.

codex.title: What Ashoka Meant by Dhamma
body: The dhamma of the edicts is conduct, not creed. It consists of: respect for parents, elders and teachers; decent treatment of servants, slaves and the poor; generosity to ascetics and brahmins of every sect; truthfulness; restraint in speech; and non-injury to living beings. Ashoka says he gave up the royal hunt, reduced animal slaughter in the kitchens, planted shade trees and dug wells along roads, built rest-houses, and appointed officers (dhamma-mahamatras) to inspect compliance.

Rock Edict 12 is the one worth memorising: it instructs people not to praise their own sect while disparaging others, and says that whoever does so out of devotion actually damages the thing they are devoted to. Ashoka was a Buddhist layman and patronised Buddhist institutions, but the edicts are not a conversion order — he funded Brahmanical, Jain and Ajivika establishments too.

codex.title: Brahmi, and How It Was Read Again
body: Brahmi is an abugida: each consonant sign carries an inherent short "a", and attached marks change the vowel. It is the ancestor of nearly every script used in South and Southeast Asia today — Devanagari, Bengali, Gurmukhi, Gujarati, Odia, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Sinhala, and through later transmission Thai, Khmer, Burmese, Lao and Balinese.

Knowledge of how to read it was lost. James Prinsep, working in Calcutta, cracked it in 1837 — helped by bilingual Indo-Greek coins that gave the same king’s name in Greek and in Brahmi, and by Christian Lassen’s parallel work. Once Brahmi could be read, Ashoka’s edicts across the subcontinent became legible and the chronology of early India could be built. A single decipherment reorganised a whole field.

codex.title: The Great Stupa at Sanchi
body: Sanchi in Madhya Pradesh has the most completely preserved early stupa complex in India. The core of Stupa 1 is Ashokan brick; it was enlarged in stone in the second century BCE, and the four carved gateways (toranas) that everyone photographs are later still, of the Satavahana period around the first century BCE.

The carvings are a primary source in their own right. They show crowded city scenes, ships, musicians, stories from the Buddha’s previous lives, and — importantly — they depict the Buddha only by symbols: a footprint, an empty seat, a wheel, a tree. Figural images of the Buddha appear later, at Mathura and Gandhara. Hundreds of short donor inscriptions name the people who paid for individual railings, and a striking number of them are women, merchants and ordinary monks rather than kings.

codex.title: The Parts of a Stupa
body: From the ground up: a circular drum or terrace (medhi), the solid hemispherical dome (anda) which encloses a relic chamber, a square railed box on top (harmika), a central mast (yashti) carrying tiered parasols (chhatra). Around it runs a stone railing (vedika) enclosing a circumambulation path (pradakshina patha), entered through carved gateways (toranas), usually at the four cardinal directions.

The plan explains the practice. A stupa is solid — you cannot go inside — so the ritual is to walk around it clockwise, and the architecture exists to organise that walk. The parasols mark honour, the mast the axis, the railing the boundary between ordinary and sacred ground. The form travelled and mutated: into the dagobas of Sri Lanka, the chedis of Thailand, the chortens of Tibet, Borobudur in Java, and the pagodas of China and Japan.

codex.title: Pataliputra
body: Modern Patna sits on top of it, which is why we know Pataliputra mostly in fragments. Excavations have found a massive timber palisade — wooden city walls, matching the Greek descriptions — and an enormous pillared hall at Kumrahar whose polished sandstone columns suggest Mauryan royal work.

Megasthenes, Seleucid ambassador to Chandragupta’s court around 302 BCE, described the city as wall-and-moat defended with hundreds of towers and dozens of gates. His account, the Indica, survives only as quotations in later Greek writers, so it must be used carefully. The city’s advantages were geographic: the confluence of the Ganga with the Son and other rivers, controlling river traffic, iron from the south of Magadha, elephants from the forests, and very fertile land.

codex.title: The Arthashastra
codex.when: Compiled c. 2nd century BCE – 3rd century CE
body: A treatise on statecraft in fifteen books, traditionally ascribed to Kautilya (identified with Chanakya, Chandragupta’s adviser). The surviving text is probably a compilation reaching its final form some centuries after the Mauryas, so it should be read as the accumulated science of government rather than as a Mauryan policy document.

It is relentlessly practical and frequently uncomfortable: chapters on taxation and land revenue, irrigation works, mining, weights and measures, famine relief, criminal procedure, torture, the recruitment and management of spies, the treatment of conquered populations, and the circles of alliance between neighbouring states. It is not a book about what is right; it is a book about what works for a ruler — which is exactly why reading it alongside Ashoka’s edicts is so instructive.

codex.title: How the Empire Paid for Itself
body: Land revenue was the backbone — a share of the harvest, conventionally around one-sixth but variable, assessed by officials on surveyed land. On top of that came tolls at city gates and on roads, mint and mining royalties (the state claimed mines), irrigation cess, forest produce, and taxes on crafts and trade. Punch-marked silver coins circulated widely.

The administration described in the Arthashastra and visible in the edicts includes a graded bureaucracy, granaries against famine, state workshops, and inspectors. Ashoka’s pillar edicts mention road-building, wells and rest-houses at intervals, and the planting of shade and fruit trees. An empire of that size is held together far more by logistics and record-keeping than by armies.

codex.title: The Gupta Period
body: A smaller, looser empire than the Mauryan one, built on tributary arrangements rather than direct rule, and remembered for what was produced under it: Aryabhata’s astronomy, Varahamihira’s compendia, Kalidasa’s plays and poems, the maturing of decimal place-value notation, the Ajanta paintings, and some of the finest early stone sculpture in India. The Allahabad pillar inscription by the poet Harisena lists Samudragupta’s campaigns.

The "golden age" label needs care. The achievements are real and the patronage was real, but the same period shows the hardening of caste restrictions in the legal literature and a decline in women’s property rights in those texts. Gupta gold coinage is superb, and gold coinage is not a measure of how most people lived. Golden ages are usually golden for somebody in particular.

codex.title: Nalanda Mahavihara
body: Founded under Gupta patronage in the fifth century CE and running for roughly seven hundred years, Nalanda was a residential monastic university in Bihar. The excavated site shows rows of multi-storeyed brick viharas — individual cells around courtyards — facing a line of temples, with a library complex that later Tibetan sources call Dharmaganja.

The curriculum went well beyond Buddhist doctrine: logic and debate, Sanskrit grammar, medicine, metaphysics, mathematics and astronomy. Students came from Tibet, China, Korea, Central Asia, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and admission involved an oral examination at the gate that reportedly turned most applicants away. The Chinese monk Xuanzang studied there in the 630s and his travel account is one of our best descriptions of the place.

It declined with the loss of royal patronage and was sacked during the Ghurid campaigns in Bihar around 1193. The site was inscribed by UNESCO in 2016, and a modern university nearby has taken the name.

codex.title: The Great Temple at Thanjavur
body: Rajaraja I’s temple — Rajarajesvaram, now usually called Brihadeeswarar — has a vimana (tower over the sanctum) about 66 m high, built of granite in diminishing storeys, crowned by a monolithic capstone weighing on the order of 80 tonnes. There is no mortar in the tower: the blocks are cut to interlock and are held by weight and geometry.

Granite is not local to the Kaveri delta, so the stone was quarried and moved a considerable distance. Local tradition holds that the ramp used to raise the capstone began several kilometres away at a village still called Sarapallam, "the hollow of the scaffold". The temple has stood through earthquakes for over a thousand years and is part of the UNESCO "Great Living Chola Temples" inscription — "living" because worship never stopped.

codex.title: Building Without Mortar
body: Dravida towers of this period are corbelled, not arched: each course of stone steps slightly inward, so the load travels down through the mass rather than around a curve. That means the tower must be very thick at the base and that the stones must be dressed to fit precisely, because any gap concentrates stress.

The temple has no deep foundation in the modern sense. Instead a broad compacted platform spreads the load across soft alluvial soil — the same strategy a wide snowshoe uses. The practical tools were ramps on shallow gradients, timber rollers, levers, ropes and very large numbers of people. No machine in the sequence is clever; the intelligence is in the geometry and the organisation of labour.

codex.title: Chola Bronzes
body: Chola bronzes are among the great achievements of world sculpture: Shiva as Nataraja in a ring of flame, Parvati, the saints of the Tamil bhakti tradition, Rama and Sita. They were made as processional images — carried out of the temple on festival days — so they have lugs for poles and are engineered to balance when lifted.

The alloy is a copper base with tin and small amounts of other metals; the texts speak of pancha-loha, five metals. The Nataraja form is both theology and statics: a figure balanced on one foot inside a ring, with the raised leg, the hair and the arms counterweighting each other. Bronze casting continues today in the same district, around Swamimalai, using the same method.

codex.title: Lost-Wax Casting
codex.when: c. 2500 BCE onward in South Asia
body: Madhuchchhishta vidhana — the "lost beeswax method". Model the figure in wax, often over a clay core. Coat it in fine clay, then coarser clay, leaving channels. Fire the mould so the wax melts and runs out, leaving a cavity exactly the shape of the model. Pour in molten bronze. Let it cool, break the mould away, then chase and polish the surface.

The mould is destroyed to release the casting, which means every solid-cast bronze made this way is unique — there is no reusable mould. The technique is very old in South Asia: the small bronze figure from Mohenjo-daro usually called the "Dancing Girl" was made this way around 2500 BCE, roughly three and a half millennia before the Chola workshops.

codex.title: The Uttaramerur Inscriptions
body: On the walls of the Vaikunta Perumal temple at Uttaramerur in Tamil Nadu, inscriptions from the reign of Parantaka I set out in detail how the village assembly chose its committees. The village was divided into wards; eligible men were nominated; the names were written on palm-leaf tickets, put into a pot (kudam), and drawn out by a young boy — the kudavolai, or pot-ticket, system.

The qualifications include owning tax-paying land, living in a house on one’s own site, an age range, and knowledge of prescribed texts. The disqualifications are longer and more revealing: anyone who has not submitted his accounts, or whose relatives have not, or who has served in the last three years, or who has been convicted of certain offences, is barred. So: written rules, property and literacy qualifications, compulsory audit, a lottery, and term limits — in the tenth century. It is not universal suffrage, and calling it "ancient democracy" oversells it; the genuine achievement is rule-bound, auditable, rotating local government.

codex.title: How the Chola State Worked
body: Below the king sat a layered structure: mandalams (provinces), valanadus and nadus (districts), and at the base self-governing local bodies — the ur for ordinary villages, the sabha or mahasabha for brahmadeya villages, and the nagaram for merchant towns. Land was surveyed and classified for revenue; irrigation works were maintained collectively.

Almost everything we know comes from inscriptions, mostly on temple walls, recording grants, wages, measurements and disputes. That gives us unusual detail about ordinary administration — and a systematic bias: temple walls record what donors wanted remembered, and are silent about famines, revolts and the people with nothing to donate.

codex.title: Life in a Chola Village
body: Temple inscriptions list the people a large temple employed and paid: priests, accountants, garland-makers, drummers, singers of the Tamil hymns, dancers, lamp-lighters, potters, carpenters, watchmen. They record exact allowances in paddy and land. This makes a big temple legible as an economic institution — employer, landowner, bank and granary — as much as a religious one.

The same inscriptions record the devadasi institution, and modern historians read it in sharply different ways depending on period and evidence. The social order was hierarchical and that hierarchy is visible in the records: who may enter which enclosure, who receives which share. A Chola village is worth studying precisely because the documentation is good enough to show both the organisation and the inequality.

codex.title: The Chola Fleet
body: Rajendra I sent a naval expedition across the Bay of Bengal against Srivijaya around 1025 CE. The Thanjavur inscriptions list the ports taken, which is how we know it happened at all. The target was the Strait of Malacca — the chokepoint through which all China trade passed — and the aim was leverage over that trade rather than settlement.

The Cholas also took Sri Lanka and raided the Maldives, and maintained diplomatic and commercial contact with Song China, where Chola embassies are recorded. Behind the fleet stood the great merchant guilds — the Ayyavole Five Hundred and the Manigramam — whose inscriptions turn up as far away as Sumatra. Medieval South India was a maritime power, which is the part of the story most often left out of textbooks.

codex.title: Sailing on a Schedule the Sky Sets
body: The Indian Ocean monsoon reverses twice a year: south-westerly roughly June to September, north-easterly roughly November to February. That makes the ocean unusually predictable for sail — and it means voyages had fixed seasons. A ship leaving the Coromandel coast for Southeast Asia sailed east on the north-east monsoon and could not return until the winds turned.

The consequence is cultural, not just commercial. Crews and merchants wintered in foreign ports for months at a time, and ideas, scripts, religions, architectural styles and epics travelled with them. The spread of the Ramayana, of Buddhism, and of Brahmi-derived scripts across Southeast Asia all ride on this wind pattern. The first-century Greek handbook Periplus of the Erythraean Sea already describes the timings.

codex.title: Tanks, Temples and Water
body: Peninsular India has a seasonal monsoon and hard rock geology, so storing rain matters more than diverting rivers. The answer, developed over millennia, was the tank: an earthen or masonry bund across a shallow valley, catching runoff and releasing it through sluices into fields, with chains of tanks arranged so that the overflow from one feeds the next.

Tanks were built and maintained by villages, temples and kings; Chola and later inscriptions record repairs, desilting duties and the penalties for neglect. The temple tank — the pushkarani or kalyani — was both a ritual bathing place and part of this water system. India’s traditional water structures run from Harappan reservoirs at Dholavira to the stepwells of Gujarat and Rajasthan and the tank cascades of Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, and many of them still work.

codex.title: The Sun Temple at Konark
body: Built under Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty, the temple is conceived as the chariot of the sun: twenty-four great carved wheels along the plinth and seven horses straining at the front. European sailors called it the Black Pagoda and used it as a landmark.

The main tower (deul), once perhaps 70 m high, collapsed — the causes are debated, with candidates including structural failure, subsidence and later damage. The great porch (jagamohana) survives, filled in during a nineteenth-century intervention to stop it following the tower down. The sculpture ranges from musicians and dancers to erotic panels to extremely precise animal carving, and it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1984).

codex.title: The Wheels Are Sundials
body: Konark’s wheels are about 3 m across, with eight broad major spokes and eight slender minor spokes between them, and a raised hub with an axle. Place a finger or a rod at the axle and the shadow it throws across the rim marks time: eight major spokes divide the daylight into eight parts of roughly three hours, and the minor spokes halve those again. Beads carved along the rim subdivide further.

This is why the symmetry matters. A dial whose spokes are unevenly spaced reads a different time on each side. The precision of the carving is therefore not decoration; it is calibration. Local guides still demonstrate the reading, and visitors still check it against their phones — which is a pleasing way to find out that it works.

codex.title: The Kalinga Temple Idiom
body: Odisha developed a distinctive branch of the Nagara family. Its signature is the rekha deul: a tower whose walls rise almost vertically before curving sharply inward near the top, capped by a flat amalaka disc and a kalasha. In front stands a pyramidal-roofed hall, the jagamohana, and larger complexes add dance and offering halls in a line.

The Lingaraja at Bhubaneswar, the Jagannath temple at Puri, Mukteshwara, Rajarani and Konark are the landmarks of the idiom. Odisha also preserves an unusually rich body of architectural manuals (silpa texts) written by and for the builders, which lets us read the buildings using their own vocabulary rather than one invented later.

codex.title: Aryabhata
body: Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya at twenty-three: four chapters, 121 verses, extremely compressed. In it he argues that the apparent daily rotation of the heavens is caused by the Earth turning on its own axis — using the image of a passenger in a moving boat seeing the bank slide past — and gives the length of the sidereal day as 23 hours 56 minutes and about 4.1 seconds, which is accurate.

He explains lunar and solar eclipses as shadows cast by the Earth and the Moon, with methods to compute their size and duration, rejecting the demon-swallowing account. He gives a sine table (his jya values are the origin, via Arabic, of our word "sine"), a method for extracting square and cube roots, and the value 62,832/20,000 = 3.1416 for π — labelled asanna, "approximate", which is the intellectually honest part.

He was not uncontradicted. Brahmagupta, a century later, attacked several of his positions, and some of those criticisms were right. That argument is the evidence that this was a working scientific tradition rather than a set of pronouncements.

codex.title: Zero and the Ten Digits
body: Place-value notation needs a symbol for an empty position, and treating that symbol as a number in its own right is a further step. Brahmagupta’s Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE) is the first known text to set out the arithmetic of zero and of negative quantities — which he explains in terms of fortunes and debts — including the rules for addition, subtraction and multiplication, and the observation that division by zero does not yield a usable result.

For the written symbol, the Gwalior inscription of 876 CE gives a clear decimal zero as a digit; the Bakhshali manuscript contains dot-zeros but its date is contested across several centuries. From India the system passed to the Islamic world — al-Khwarizmi and al-Kindi wrote about "Hindu reckoning" in the ninth century — and from there to Europe, where Fibonacci popularised it in 1202. English still calls the digits Hindu-Arabic, which is an unusually accurate piece of naming.

codex.title: The Kerala School
body: A lineage of mathematician-astronomers in a cluster of villages in central Kerala, beginning with Madhava of Sangamagrama (c. 1340–1425) and continuing through Parameshvara, Nilakantha Somayaji, Jyeshthadeva and Achyuta Pisharati. Madhava obtained infinite series expansions for the sine, cosine and arctangent functions, and a series for π with correction terms that converge usefully — results that in Europe are associated with Newton, Leibniz, Gregory and Taylor two to three centuries later.

Jyeshthadeva’s Yuktibhasha (c. 1530), written in Malayalam rather than Sanskrit, is remarkable because it gives *derivations*, not just results — something close to proof, including an early treatment of what we would call term-by-term integration. Whether any of this reached Europe through Jesuit contacts in Kerala is an open and actively researched question; the mathematics itself is not in doubt.

codex.title: The Siddhanta Tradition
body: A siddhanta is a comprehensive astronomical treatise: planetary models, eclipse computation, geography, instruments and timekeeping. The canon runs through the Surya Siddhanta, Aryabhata’s Aryabhatiya, Varahamihira’s Pancha-siddhantika (which usefully surveys five earlier systems), Brahmagupta, Bhaskara I and Bhaskara II’s Siddhanta Shiromani, and the Kerala texts.

The tradition had distinctive working habits. Results were written in compressed verse for memorisation; successive authors wrote commentaries that corrected their predecessors and said so; and models were judged against observation, with tables revised when predictions drifted. It also absorbed and argued with outside work — Greek and later Islamic astronomy — rather than ignoring it. Sawai Jai Singh’s eighteenth-century observatories are the last great flowering of this habit of mind.

codex.title: Jantar Mantar
body: Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber built five observatories — at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi. The Jaipur one survives best and holds about twenty masonry instruments. The Samrat Yantra there is an enormous right-triangle gnomon, roughly 27 m high, with curved quadrant scales on either side; it reads local solar time to within a couple of seconds.

Jai Singh had Euclid and Ptolemy translated into Sanskrit, obtained European astronomical tables and telescopes, and compared them against Indian and Islamic ones, publishing where they disagreed. He then built in stone on purpose: a shadow cast across a 27 m scale can be read far more finely than one on a small brass instrument. The site was inscribed by UNESCO in 2010.

Other instruments measure different quantities: the Ram Yantra gives altitude and azimuth, the Jai Prakash Yantra maps the sun onto complementary sunken hemispheres, the Chakra Yantra reads declination and hour angle, the Narivalaya has dials for either side of the equinox, and the Rashivalaya is twelve separate instruments, one per zodiac sign.

codex.title: Measuring the Sky Without a Telescope
body: Before the telescope, positional astronomy depended on angle measurement, and angle measurement depended on size: a larger instrument has a longer arc, so each degree occupies more physical space and can be subdivided more finely. That is why pre-telescopic observatories — Maragheh, Samarkand under Ulugh Beg, Tycho Brahe’s Uraniborg, and Jai Singh’s Jantar Mantars — all tend towards the monumental.

The core quantities were: the altitude of a body above the horizon, its azimuth around the horizon, the local time from a shadow, the moment of a transit across a meridian, and the declination of a star. From long series of these, built up over years, you get planetary periods, calendar corrections and eclipse predictions. Patient repetition, not any single observation, is what makes the tables good.

codex.title: A City Built in a Boulder Field
body: Hampi sits on the Tungabhadra among granite hills weathered into enormous rounded boulders. The rock is some of the oldest exposed on Earth — part of the Dharwar craton — and the shapes come from millions of years of exfoliation, the outer shells of the rock peeling away like onion layers.

Vijayanagara’s builders used the landscape rather than levelling it. Boulders become gateways, foundations, temple walls and defensive lines; quarry marks and rows of wedge holes are visible on hundreds of them. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1986) and still an active landscape of villages, banana fields and canals.

codex.title: Virupaksha Temple
body: Virupaksha is older than the empire that made it famous — a shrine existed here before 1336 — and it was enlarged repeatedly, most grandly under Krishnadevaraya in the early sixteenth century, who added the great eastern gopuram and the pillared hall. In front of it runs the long colonnaded bazaar street that served pilgrims and traders.

It is still in daily worship, which makes it one of the very few parts of Vijayanagara that never became a ruin. That continuity is itself a historical fact worth noticing: the destruction of 1565 was devastating and it was not total.

codex.title: The Stone Chariot
body: In the Vittala temple courtyard stands the famous stone chariot — in fact a shrine to Garuda, built in the shape of a processional chariot. It is not carved from a single block, as is often claimed: it is assembled from several granite pieces, and the joints are visible once you know to look. Its wheels were once able to turn; they have since been fixed in place to prevent damage.

The same complex holds the so-called musical pillars: clusters of slender colonettes carved from single blocks, which ring at different pitches when tapped. They are structural columns that also resonate — the pitch depends on the dimensions of each colonette. Decades of visitors striking them with coins and hands caused real harm, and touching them is now restricted.

codex.title: The Water System
body: Vijayanagara depended on engineered water. A diversion weir (anicut) on the Tungabhadra fed gravity canals, some cut through solid rock, carrying water to fields, tanks and the royal centre. Raised aqueducts crossed low ground; settling basins dropped silt; sluices distributed the flow. Inside the royal enclosure, the stepped tank excavated in the 1980s is built from pre-cut blocks carrying mason’s numbers — a kit assembled on site.
Several of these canals were never abandoned and still irrigate the fields around Kamalapura today. For a city famous for being destroyed, its most durable legacy turns out to be its plumbing.

codex.title: Farming a Hard Country
body: The Deccan plateau has thin soils, hard rock and a monsoon that arrives in a few violent months. Agriculture there has always been an exercise in storage: bunded tanks across shallow valleys, chains of tanks feeding one another, wells, and in the black-soil tracts dry-farming techniques for sorghum, millets, pulses and cotton.

Vijayanagara-period inscriptions record the building and repair of tanks as acts of merit, and assign responsibility for desilting. Where river water was reachable, as at Hampi, canals supplemented the tanks. Rice and sugarcane in the irrigated pockets, millets everywhere else — a pattern that still largely describes the region.

codex.title: The Bazaars
body: Long colonnaded streets run in front of the major temples, excavated and still traceable, with stone platforms and pillared shop fronts. Both Persian and Portuguese visitors describe markets selling pepper, textiles, gems, horses, perfumes, precious metals and slaves, and describe foreign merchant quarters within the city.

The currency was a gold coin the Portuguese called the pagoda — the varaha — with smaller gold and silver panams and copper jitals for everyday use. Revenue came from land, customs at gates, market dues and tribute from feudatory chiefs. The bazaars were physically attached to temples because temples were economic institutions: landowners, employers, and holders of endowments.

codex.title: The Horse Problem
body: The Deccan does not breed good cavalry horses — climate, fodder and disease all work against it — so warhorses had to be imported from Arabia, Persia and Central Asia. That single fact shaped Deccan politics for centuries: Vijayanagara and the sultanates of Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Golconda competed continuously for a supply they did not control.

When the Portuguese took Goa in 1510 they grasped the leverage immediately and used licensing of the horse trade as a diplomatic instrument with every Deccan power. Krishnadevaraya negotiated with them over exactly this. It is a useful corrective to thinking of military history as battles: the decisive constraint here was logistics and animal husbandry.

codex.title: The Court of Krishnadevaraya
body: Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva line is the empire’s best-remembered ruler: a successful campaigner, a builder, and an author. His Telugu poem Amuktamalyada includes a passage of practical advice on governing — on treating the peasantry well, on managing ports and foreign merchants, on the uses of conciliation.

He patronised poets in Telugu, Sanskrit, Kannada and Tamil, and the ashtadiggajas, the "eight elephants" of his Telugu literary circle, are remembered by name. The court was multilingual as a matter of course. The royal centre at Hampi mixes architectural idioms freely — arches and domes beside Dravidian brackets and chhatris — which is the architecture of a state that employed people from everywhere.

codex.title: How We Know What We Know About Hampi
body: Three independent bodies of evidence, each with its own bias. Inscriptions: precisely dated, narrow, and recording only what donors wanted recorded — a wall full of pious grants will never mention a famine or a tax revolt. Foreign accounts: Abdur Razzaq (1443), Niccolò de’ Conti, Domingo Paes and Fernão Nuniz (1520s), all vivid and all written by men with reasons to exaggerate a kingdom’s wealth. And the archaeology: the long Vijayanagara Research Project survey, which mapped canals, bazaars, roads and enclosures.

Several famous names are modern inventions. "Lotus Mahal", "Queen’s Bath", "Elephant Stables" are nineteenth-century labels, not Vijayanagara terms, and their functions are argued from plan and position. Where inscriptions, travellers and archaeology converge — the irrigation canals, the Mahanavami festival platform, the colonnaded bazaars — we are on firm ground. Where they conflict, that is where the research question is.

codex.title: 1565 and After
body: In January 1565 a coalition of the Deccan sultanates — Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar — defeated the Vijayanagara army at the battle usually called Talikota (also Rakshasa-Tangadi). The commander Rama Raya was killed, the army broke, and the capital was plundered.

The later chronicles describe one total catastrophe. The archaeology is more complicated: heavy burning and deliberate destruction in some quarters, continuity in others, and worship at Virupaksha that never stopped. The dynasty itself continued from Penukonda and then Chandragiri for decades. The capital’s abandonment was real and it was a process — the loss of a defeated city’s reason to exist — rather than a single afternoon. History usually runs slower than the story told about it afterwards.

codex.title: The Taj Mahal
body: Built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 at Burhanpur. The chief architect is generally credited as Ustad Ahmad Lahauri. The white marble is from Makrana in Rajasthan, roughly 400 km away; the inlay stones came from much further — carnelian, jasper, lapis lazuli, jade, turquoise.

The engineering is as interesting as the romance. The tomb stands on well foundations of timber and rubble beside the Yamuna, which keeps the timber permanently wet and therefore sound. The dome is double-shelled. The four minarets lean very slightly outward, so that if they ever failed they would fall away from the tomb. The calligraphic panels use letters that grow taller as they rise, so they appear uniform from the ground.
One deliberate asymmetry breaks an otherwise perfectly bilateral building: Mumtaz’s cenotaph sits on the central axis, and Shah Jahan’s, added later, does not.

codex.title: The Double Dome
body: A tall dome looks right on a skyline and feels oppressive from inside; a dome sized for the interior looks squat from outside. The double dome solves both at once: an inner shell proportioned to the chamber below, and an outer shell proportioned to the building’s silhouette, with a void between them.

The technique reached India through Timurid Central Asia and appears in Indian buildings from the fifteenth century, maturing at Humayun’s Tomb and then at the Taj. The same logic was arrived at independently elsewhere — Brunelleschi’s dome in Florence is double-shelled too. When you stand under the Taj’s dome you are not looking at the dome you photographed from the garden.

codex.title: Parchin Kari
body: Parchin kari — known in Europe as pietra dura — is stone inlay: semi-precious stones cut to shape and set into recesses chiselled out of marble, fitted so closely that the joints are invisible to a running fingertip. A single flower spray on the Taj can contain dozens of separate pieces.

The designs are built on fourfold symmetry, which means a craftsman designs and proves one quadrant and repeats it. The craft did not stop: workshops in Agra still practise it, and many of the families doing so trace their trade to the imperial ateliers.

codex.title: The Charbagh
body: Char bagh means "four gardens": a square divided into quadrants by raised walkways carrying water channels, with a tank or pavilion where the axes cross. Each quadrant is often quartered again, so the pattern repeats at smaller scale. The form came from Persia and Timurid Central Asia and was adapted in India at Humayun’s Tomb and then at the Taj.

It is irrigation as much as symbolism. The channels water the beds, the raised walkways keep feet dry, and the sunken quadrants let tree canopies sit at eye level from the path. At the Taj the tomb sits at the end of the garden rather than at its centre, which is unusual and still argued over.

codex.title: Reading a Mughal Building
body: You can usually date a Mughal building by its material and its openings. Akbar’s period favours red sandstone, trabeate construction — flat lintels carried on brackets — chhatris, and decorative vocabulary borrowed from Rajput and Gujarati builders. Shah Jahan’s period favours white marble, cusped arches, bulbous domes and pietra dura.

Both are synthetic styles rather than imported ones. The pointed arch, the dome and the charbagh arrive from Central Asia and Persia; the bracket, the chhatri, the carved corbel and much of the craft labour are Indian. Fatehpur Sikri is the clearest single place to see the two traditions being argued out in stone.

codex.title: Fatehpur Sikri
body: Akbar built a complete capital in red sandstone 40 km from Agra: the Diwan-i-Khas with its extraordinary central pillar and radiating bridges, the five-storey Panch Mahal, the Jama Masjid with the enormous Buland Darwaza, and the Ibadat Khana where the religious debates were held.

It was effectively abandoned within about fifteen years. Water is the usual explanation — the lake that supplied it was unreliable — though political and strategic reasons are also argued. It survives unusually intact precisely because nobody kept rebuilding it, which makes it one of the best-preserved sixteenth-century cities anywhere.

codex.title: Sulh-i-Kul
body: Akbar convened scholars of several traditions — Muslim ulama, Brahmin pandits, Jain munis, Zoroastrian priests, and Jesuits from Goa — for debates in the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri. He abolished the pilgrimage tax and the jizya on non-Muslims, married into Rajput houses, and appointed Hindus including Raja Todar Mal and Raja Man Singh to the highest offices.

The policy was formulated as sulh-i-kul, "peace with all": not that all religions are the same, but that the state should not take sides and that no one should revile another’s faith. Abu’l Fazl articulated it; the court historian Badauni, who thought Akbar a heretic, kept his post and translated the Mahabharata anyway.

The limits matter as much as the achievement. This was the policy of one ruler, not a constitutional settlement, and Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya in 1679. A tolerance that depends on the character of a king is only ever on loan.

codex.title: The Translation Bureau
body: Akbar — who could not read, and had everything read aloud to him — ran a maktab khana that translated Sanskrit works into Persian. The Mahabharata became the Razmnama, lavishly illustrated. The Ramayana, the Atharva Veda, the Yoga Vasistha, the Panchatantra and Bhaskara’s Lilavati were all translated.

The painting workshops did something similar with images, combining Persian line and composition with Indian colour and observation. Basawan and Daswanth worked under Akbar; later Mansur painted birds and animals so precisely that naturalists still cite him, and Bichitr produced political allegory of real subtlety. The Ain-i-Akbari, Abu’l Fazl’s administrative gazetteer, belongs to the same project of writing everything down.

codex.title: Twenty Thousand People
body: Contemporary accounts and surviving records describe a workforce of roughly twenty thousand over two decades: quarrymen at Makrana, bullock teams and specially built ramps to move marble, masons, inlay specialists, calligraphers, scaffolders, water-carriers and the clerks who paid them. Some are named in the ledgers; most are not.

A workmen’s settlement grew next to the site and became the neighbourhood still called Taj Ganj. The frequently repeated story that the workers’ hands were cut off afterwards has no contemporary evidence behind it and is rejected by historians — which is worth knowing, because a building this famous attracts invented stories as reliably as it attracts visitors.

codex.title: Stepwells and Baolis
body: A stepwell is a well you walk down into: flights of steps descending several storeys to the water table, so that the supply stays reachable as the level drops through the dry season. Gujarat and Rajasthan have the most elaborate — Rani ki Vav at Patan, with sculpture on every level, and Chand Baori at Abhaneri with some 3,500 steps.

They are also architecture for climate. Twenty metres down, out of the sun, the air is many degrees cooler, and stepwells served as rest stops, meeting places and shelters as much as water sources. Many were commissioned by women, and their inscriptions say so. Most fell out of use when piped supply arrived, and a number are now being restored — partly for heritage, partly because groundwater recharge has become urgent again.

codex.title: The Logic of a Hill Fort
body: A giri-durga — hill fort — turns terrain into a weapon. The approach is a long exposed climb, so an attacker is under fire for an hour before reaching anything. The gate is set at a right angle inside a passage, so no elephant or ram can build momentum against it. Bastions project from the wall so defenders shoot *along* the face rather than straight out, covering the ground the attacker has to cross. And the water is inside, cut into the rock.

Rajasthan’s hill forts — Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh with its 36 km wall, Ranthambore, Gagron, Amber, Jaisalmer — were inscribed together by UNESCO in 2013. Shivaji’s Sahyadri forts work on the same principles at smaller scale but in far greater numbers: a network, where losing one fort means walking to the next.

codex.title: Sieges Are Decided by Water
body: Every serious hill fort has cisterns cut into living rock — roofed or deeply sunk against evaporation, filled by the monsoon, and sized for a year or more of occupation. Raigad, Sinhagad, Kumbhalgarh and Chittorgarh all have substantial tank systems, and some are still full.

This is why water is the first thing a besieger looks for and the first thing a fort architect solves. Walls can be repaired under fire; a dry cistern cannot be refilled in June. Most dramatic siege stories are, underneath, hydrology.

codex.title: The Tower of Victory
body: Rana Kumbha of Mewar raised the Vijaya Stambha at Chittorgarh — nine storeys, around 37 m, with projecting balconies and sculpture on every level, and a narrow internal stair. It commemorates a victory over the Sultan of Malwa, and it is also a genealogical record: inscriptions inside list the rulers of the house.

Kumbha is credited with a remarkable amount of building, including Kumbhalgarh, whose perimeter wall is among the longest in the world. Chittorgarh itself covers some 280 hectares on a plateau and is the largest fort in India.

codex.title: Haldighati and After
body: Maharana Pratap of Mewar met a Mughal force commanded by Raja Man Singh of Amber in a narrow pass at Haldighati in June 1576. Both sides claimed the day; the battle was tactically inconclusive, Pratap escaped, and the Mughals took Gogunda but could not hold the countryside.

What followed matters more than the battle. Pratap spent years fighting a mobile campaign from the hills, avoiding set-piece engagements, and recovered most of Mewar — including Kumbhalgarh — before his death in 1597. The two traditions remember it differently: Rajput bardic sources as a heroic stand, Mughal chronicles as a victory. Reading both is the only honest way to handle it, and it is a good early example of the asymmetric method the Marathas would later systematise.

codex.title: Ganimi Kava
body: Shivaji’s doctrine, usually translated as guerrilla warfare, though "war of movement" is closer. Strike supply columns and paymasters rather than armoured centres. Fight at night and in the ghats where cavalry and artillery cannot manoeuvre. Use the monsoon, which immobilises a heavy army from June to September while light infantry still walks. Rely on local men who know every track because they were born on it.
