It is not a substitute for organisation but a product of it: intelligence networks, a fort system within signalling distance, and a disciplined light infantry drawn from the Mawal valleys. Pratapgad in 1659 and Sinhagad in 1670 are the showpieces; the Agra escape of 1666 belongs to the same habit of mind.

codex.title: A Navy Nobody Expected
body: Shivaji understood something most contemporary Indian land powers did not: a coast without a fleet is a door without a latch. The Siddis held Janjira, the Portuguese Goa, the English Bombay, and any of them could land where they chose. So he built sea forts — Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg on offshore rock — and a fleet of smaller, faster vessels to escort Maratha merchants and harass others.

The institution outlived him. Kanhoji Angre, as Sarkhel, held the Konkan coast for three decades against Portuguese, Dutch and English squadrons, taking prizes and levying his own tolls. Indian naval history is badly under-taught, and this is the clearest case of it.

codex.title: The Council of Eight
body: Shivaji’s state was run by the Ashta Pradhan: Peshwa for general administration, Amatya for finance and accounts, Sachiv for correspondence, Mantri for intelligence and the royal household, Senapati for the army, Sumant for foreign affairs, Nyayadhish for justice, and Panditrao for religious endowments and charity.

They were intended as offices rather than hereditary gifts, and court records were kept in Marathi and Sanskrit rather than Persian. The intention did not hold: within two generations the Peshwa’s office had become hereditary and the real power in the state. Institutions drift, and watching this one drift is more instructive than any single battle.

codex.title: Taxing Instead of Looting
body: Chauth and sardeshmukhi were assessed shares — conventionally a quarter and a tenth of revenue — collected against land measurement with written receipts, not improvised plunder. Shivaji’s standing orders to his own commanders forbid touching the standing crop, the cattle or the women of a village, and officers were punished for breaches.

The reasoning is economic, not sentimental: a soldier who burns a village has destroyed next year’s revenue to feed himself today. The Mawal villages that supplied his infantry had to remain farms. This is also where the later empire ran into trouble, as chauth collection across distant territories drifted closer to extraction the further it got from home.

codex.title: Ahilyabai Holkar
body: Widowed and then bereaved of her son, Ahilyabai took over the Holkar state of Malwa and ruled it for nearly thirty years from Maheshwar on the Narmada. She is remembered almost entirely for public works: ghats, wells, roads, rest-houses and temples from Varanasi to Somnath to Rameswaram, including the rebuilding of the Kashi Vishwanath temple in 1780.

She also held the state together militarily and administratively in a crowded and hostile Deccan, and heard petitions in person. The contrast with the better-known Maratha story is the point: the most durable things any of these rulers built were not victories.

codex.title: 1761: Why Panipat Was Lost
body: The Maratha army under Sadashivrao Bhau met Ahmad Shah Durrani’s forces at Panipat in January 1761 and was destroyed. The casualties were enormous and the political damage lasting.

The battle itself was decided less by tactics than by everything around it. The Marathas were operating a thousand kilometres from their base, with supply lines cut, provisions exhausted and a huge non-combatant train to feed. The allies they expected — the Rajputs, the Jats, Awadh — were largely absent or hostile, partly because of how chauth had been collected from them. Durrani had better artillery and a shorter supply chain. Logistics and diplomacy lost Panipat before the fighting started, which is the lesson worth taking from it.

questions.stem: What is the most distinctive feature of a Mature Harappan city plan?
options: Streets laid out on a grid, meeting at right angles
A single ring road around a central palace
Houses radiating outward from a temple
Narrow winding lanes with no overall plan
questions.explain: Grids have to be surveyed before anything is built, which means a planning decision was taken, enforced and maintained across cities hundreds of kilometres apart.

questions.stem: Harappan bricks were made in a consistent ratio of height to width to length. What was it?
questions.explain: The 1:2:4 ratio lets bricks interlock in several bonding patterns without cutting — a standard shared across the whole Harappan area.

questions.stem: Harappan stone weights follow which numerical series?
options: Sexagesimal: 1, 60, 3600…
Fibonacci: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8…
questions.explain: The unit is about 0.856 g and the common ratio-16 weight about 13.7 g. Base 60 is Mesopotamian; the Harappans doubled instead.

questions.stem: How was the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro made watertight?
options: A layer of bitumen behind finely fitted sawn brick
Lime plaster over rubble
Glazed ceramic tiles
Sheets of beaten copper
questions.explain: It is the earliest large-scale use of bitumen waterproofing in South Asia — and the bitumen is a fact, while the tank’s ritual purpose is an inference.

questions.stem: What did Harappan cities spend their best engineering on?
options: Covered street drains and household sanitation
Royal tombs
Defensive siege walls
Temple towers
questions.explain: No contemporary city in Mesopotamia or Egypt matches the systematic coverage of Harappan drainage, and nothing in the subcontinent matches it again for about two thousand years.

questions.stem: Why has the Indus script resisted decipherment?
options: No bilingual text, very short inscriptions, and the language is unknown
The tablets were all destroyed in antiquity
It was deciphered in 1952 but the results are classified
The signs are purely decorative and encode nothing
questions.explain: Every successful decipherment has needed a bilingual text, known names or language, and enough text to test ideas. The Indus script offers none of the three.

questions.stem: About how long is a typical Indus inscription?
options: Around five signs
Around fifty signs
Several hundred signs
A full page of text
questions.explain: The longest known single-surface inscription is about seventeen signs. Short texts give statistical methods almost nothing to work with.

questions.stem: Which animal is the commonest motif on Indus seals?
options: A one-horned animal facing a standard or trough
The horse
The lion
The peacock
questions.explain: The absence of the horse from Indus seals, and the absence of battle scenes, are two silences historians argue about to this day.

questions.stem: Dholavira, in the Rann of Kutch, is best known for what?
options: An elaborate system of dams, channels and reservoirs
The largest Harappan granary
A royal palace with a throne room
The only Harappan site with a defensive moat
questions.explain: Dholavira sits in a near-desert between two seasonal streams, so its builders turned the city into a water-harvesting machine. It became a UNESCO site in 2021.

questions.stem: The large brick basin at Lothal is usually described as a dockyard. What is the honest position?
options: Its function is disputed — dockyard or water tank, and the evidence allows both
It is proven to be a dockyard by surviving ship timbers
It is proven to be a reservoir by an inscription
Archaeologists agree it was a swimming pool
questions.explain: S. R. Rao read it as a tidal dock; later critics read it as irrigation storage. The structure is solid evidence; its purpose is contested interpretation.

questions.stem: In Mesopotamian cuneiform records, which name is generally identified with the Indus region?
options: Meluhha
Dilmun
Magan
Elam
questions.explain: Dilmun is generally Bahrain and Magan is Oman. Meluhha lay further east and most scholars place it in the Indus world.

questions.stem: Which Indus product is found archaeologically in Mesopotamia and the Gulf?
options: Etched carnelian beads
Glass mirrors
Printed cotton with dated labels
Iron swords
questions.explain: Carnelian beads, Indus-style weights and a few seals turn up in Mesopotamia and the Gulf — physical confirmation of the trade the texts describe.

questions.stem: Why did the Harappans maintain an outpost at Shortugai in northern Afghanistan?
options: Access to lapis lazuli and tin sources
To guard a land route to Egypt
As a summer capital
To farm rice at altitude
questions.explain: Shortugai sits near the lapis sources. A trading network reaching from Gujarat to the Oxus is a serious logistical achievement for the third millennium BCE.

questions.stem: What does current evidence suggest about the end of the Harappan cities?
options: A weakening monsoon and shifting rivers led to de-urbanisation, not extinction
A single invasion destroyed every city within a decade
A volcanic eruption buried the region
The population was wiped out by plague
questions.explain: Palaeoclimate records show the monsoon weakening after about 2200 BCE; settlement surveys show people moving east and south into smaller villages. There is no destruction layer.

questions.stem: Mortimer Wheeler once read a group of Mohenjo-daro skeletons as evidence of a massacre. Why is that reading rejected now?
options: The skeletons come from different periods and mostly show no battle injuries
The skeletons were later shown to be animal bones
The excavation records were forged
They were found to be a modern burial ground
questions.explain: It is a useful lesson in reading evidence: the bones were real, the dramatic interpretation was not supported by them.

questions.stem: The small bronze figure from Mohenjo-daro known as the "Dancing Girl" was made by which technique?
options: Lost-wax casting
Hammered sheet metal
Carving from solid bronze
Pressed in a reusable iron mould
questions.explain: The same lost-wax method the Chola bronze-casters would use three and a half thousand years later. The chain of craft knowledge in the subcontinent is very long.

questions.stem: Which of these major Harappan sites lies in present-day India?
options: Rakhigarhi, in Haryana
Mohenjo-daro, in Sindh
Harappa, in Punjab (Pakistan)
Mehrgarh, in Balochistan
questions.explain: Rakhigarhi is among the largest Harappan sites. Dholavira, Lothal and Kalibangan are also in India; the civilisation straddles the modern border.

questions.stem: What have Harappan excavations conspicuously NOT produced?
options: Clearly identifiable palaces, royal tombs or temples
Evidence of writing
Standardised weights
Evidence of long-distance trade
questions.explain: We can see enormous coordinated public works but cannot identify who commanded them — one of the most interesting gaps in world archaeology.

questions.stem: Why are cuneiform signs wedge-shaped?
options: They were pressed into wet clay with a cut reed stylus
They were chiselled into granite
They were painted with a square-tipped brush
They were stamped with bronze dies
questions.explain: Latin cuneus means wedge. Pressing is faster than drawing and does not tear wet clay.

questions.stem: Cuneiform was used to write which of the following?
options: Several unrelated languages, including Sumerian, Akkadian and Old Persian
Only Sumerian
Only Akkadian
Only royal names, never full sentences
questions.explain: Cuneiform is a writing technique, not a language — rather like the Latin alphabet serving English, Turkish and Vietnamese.

questions.stem: Which inscription was the key to deciphering cuneiform?
options: The Behistun inscription, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian
The Rosetta Stone
The Great Signboard of Dholavira
The Gwalior inscription
questions.explain: Old Persian was simplest and supplied the royal names; the names supplied sound values; the sound values opened Akkadian. The Rosetta Stone did the same job for Egyptian.

questions.stem: What were the earliest substantial written documents in Mesopotamia about?
options: Accounting — quantities of barley, beer, sheep and labour
Hymns to the gods
The Epic of Gilgamesh
Astronomical predictions
questions.explain: Writing was invented to count, not to tell stories. Literature arrives centuries later and takes over the house.

questions.stem: Which everyday measurement still shows Mesopotamian base-60 counting?
options: 60 minutes in an hour and 360 degrees in a circle
The metric system
100 paise in a rupee
The 7-day week
questions.explain: Sixty divides exactly by 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12, 15, 20 and 30 — very convenient before decimal fractions were easy to write.

questions.stem: How does a ziggurat differ from an Egyptian pyramid?
options: It is a solid platform for a temple, not a tomb
It is hollow, with burial chambers inside
It is built of granite rather than brick
It has no stairs
questions.explain: A ziggurat raises a small shrine above a flat delta. It is an artificial mountain with no interior, and nobody is buried in it.

questions.stem: Why does the facing of the Ziggurat of Ur have small holes through it?
options: They are weeper holes, letting the mud-brick core dry out
They held wooden scaffolding permanently
They were arrow slits
They are damage from later quarrying
questions.explain: A baked-brick skin over a mud-brick core traps moisture, and trapped moisture destroys mud brick. The holes are a working solution to that.

questions.stem: What is notable about the penalties in Hammurabi’s law collection?
options: They are explicitly graded by the social rank of the victim
They are identical for everyone
They are all monetary fines
They apply only to priests
questions.explain: The stele is therefore a record of inequality as well as of law. Carving law publicly still matters: the rule is knowable in advance.

questions.stem: What long-term agricultural problem did Mesopotamian irrigation create?
options: Salt accumulation in the soil, pushing farmers from wheat to barley
Loss of all topsoil to wind erosion
Permanent flooding of the whole delta
Exhaustion of the fish stocks
questions.explain: Irrigating a hot, flat basin with a high water table concentrates salt. Crop records show the shift to salt-tolerant barley and falling yields in the south.

questions.stem: Dilmun, a major middleman in Gulf trade, is generally identified with which modern place?
options: Bahrain
Oman
Yemen
Cyprus
questions.explain: Magan is generally Oman. Dilmun’s role was transit: Indus goods east, Mesopotamian silver and textiles west.

questions.stem: A Mesopotamian text refers to a "Meluhhan interpreter". Why does that detail matter?
options: It implies sustained contact and a language barrier worth employing someone to bridge
It proves the Indus script has been read
It shows Meluhha spoke Sumerian
It dates the Indus civilisation precisely
questions.explain: An interpreter is evidence of regular dealings between people who could not understand each other — and a reminder that we still cannot read their script.

questions.stem: Why have so many cuneiform tablets survived?
options: Clay survives burial, and a burnt archive is baked rather than destroyed
They were all stored in sealed stone vaults
They were copied onto metal plates
Mesopotamia has no rainfall at all
questions.explain: Hundreds of thousands exist and many are still untranslated — not because they are unreadable, but because there are not enough Assyriologists.

questions.stem: Mesopotamia and the Indus were contemporaries. Why do we know so much more about Mesopotamian society?
options: Mesopotamia left a readable archive; the Indus script cannot be read
Mesopotamian cities were much larger
The Indus left no material remains
Mesopotamia has been excavated only recently
questions.explain: We know Harappan cities through bricks, drains and weights rather than words. The difference in what we can say about each is a difference in evidence, not in sophistication.

questions.stem: How many shekels made one mina in Mesopotamian reckoning?
questions.explain: An Indus merchant working in a binary weight series and a Sumerian working in sixties had to convert at the quayside.

questions.stem: How many books (kandas) make up Valmiki’s Ramayana?
options: Seven
Five
Twelve
Eighteen
questions.explain: Eighteen is the Mahabharata’s count. The Ramayana has seven kandas and roughly 24,000 verses.

questions.stem: Which two kandas do most Sanskritists regard as later additions?
options: Bala Kanda and Uttara Kanda
Aranya Kanda and Yuddha Kanda
Sundara Kanda and Kishkindha Kanda
Ayodhya Kanda and Aranya Kanda
questions.explain: The evidence is internal — differences in language, metre and the treatment of characters. Epics everywhere grew by accretion, like cities grow by layers.

questions.stem: Which book of the Ramayana is most often recited on its own, and what does it cover?
options: Sundara Kanda — Hanuman’s journey to Lanka and his meeting with Sita
Yuddha Kanda — the final battle
Bala Kanda — Rama’s childhood
Uttara Kanda — the events after the return
questions.explain: The tradition gives an entire book to reconnaissance rather than to battle, and then singles that book out for recitation. That tells you what it values.

questions.stem: Tulsidas composed the Ramcharitmanas in which language?
options: Awadhi
Sanskrit
Tamil
Bengali
questions.explain: Writing in the spoken language is the point: it is the version most north Indian households mean when they say "Ramayana", and it was never meant for scholars alone.

questions.stem: Who composed the Ramavataram, the great Tamil Ramayana?
options: Kamban
Tulsidas
Krittibas Ojha
Ezhuthachan
questions.explain: Krittibas wrote the Bengali version and Ezhuthachan the Malayalam one. Molla, a potter’s daughter, wrote a Telugu Ramayanam.

questions.stem: The Ramakien, painted along the walls of Bangkok’s royal temple, is the Ramayana of which country?
options: Thailand
Indonesia
Cambodia
Myanmar
questions.explain: Java has the Kakawin Ramayana, Cambodia the Reamker, Laos Phra Lak Phra Lam, Malaysia the Hikayat Seri Rama, Myanmar the Yama Zatdaw.

questions.stem: How did the Ramayana reach Southeast Asia?
options: With traders, monks and scholars across the Bay of Bengal over centuries
Through military conquest by Indian empires
Through nineteenth-century colonial translation
It arose independently with no connection to India
questions.explain: The monsoon made the crossing predictable and the story travelled with the cargo. Each culture then localised it — shared heritage rather than cultural export.

questions.stem: How does the Jain Paumacariya differ in its treatment of Ravana?
options: It presents him as a far more dignified, almost noble figure
It removes him from the story entirely
It makes him the narrator
It makes him Rama’s brother
questions.explain: Retellings disagree deliberately. The useful question about any version is not "is it accurate?" but "what is this teller trying to say?"

questions.stem: What is the point of the Shabari episode?
options: That the intention behind an offering outranks its ritual form
That forest dwellers must be excluded from worship
That berries are sacred fruit
That hospitality must follow strict protocol
questions.explain: She tastes each berry first to check it is not sour, which would normally make the offering improper — and it is accepted anyway. Bhakti poets return to her constantly.

questions.stem: Historians often connect the Ramayana’s forest setting to what real historical process?
options: The eastward agricultural expansion into the forested Ganga valley in the first millennium BCE
The Harappan collapse
The arrival of the Portuguese
The spread of iron ploughs from China
questions.explain: The frontier between settled farming and forest was real and contested, and the literature of the period is full of it. The epic takes forest societies seriously as political actors.

questions.stem: The Sushruta Samhita is the classical Indian compendium of which field?
options: Surgery
Astronomy
Grammar
Statecraft
questions.explain: Charaka covers internal medicine. Sushruta describes cataract couching, bladder-stone removal, and a nasal reconstruction that became the basis of modern rhinoplasty.

questions.stem: Which surgical technique travelled from India to Europe after British surgeons observed it in the eighteenth century?
options: Nasal reconstruction using a skin flap
Appendectomy
Blood transfusion
Anaesthesia using ether
questions.explain: The forehead or cheek flap method described in the Sushruta Samhita became the foundation of modern plastic surgery.

questions.stem: Why do classical Indian medical texts spend so many verses on plant identification?
options: Because misidentifying a plant can make a remedy useless or lethal
Because plants were worshipped individually
Because the texts were written for farmers
Because plant names were used as a secret code
questions.explain: Oleander and datura look harvestable and are not. Identification is the first skill a healer learns.

questions.stem: Dhanurveda is the treatise literature on what?
options: Archery and the martial arts
Temple architecture
Music theory
Land revenue
questions.explain: It describes grips, draw lengths, foot positions and the training of the eye — archery as a disciplined craft, not a knack.

questions.stem: Which best describes the scholarly view of the Ramayana tradition?
options: A field of many tellings in conversation with each other, not one original with copies
A single authoritative text with minor copying errors
A modern invention with no pre-colonial history
A translation of a Greek original
questions.explain: A. K. Ramanujan’s essay on this is the standard reference point, and the title everybody remembers is "Three Hundred Ramayanas".

questions.stem: What do marine surveys show about the shoal chain between Rameswaram and Mannar?
options: It is a natural chain of sandbanks, beach ridges and coral, far older than any human record
It is a continuous artificial causeway of dressed stone
It is a modern dredging spoil bank
It does not exist and appears only on old charts
questions.explain: The shoal is real and much of it is walkable at low tide. It is natural, and the epic account is culturally meaningful. Both can be true; they are different kinds of claim.

questions.stem: In Valmiki’s account, who directs the building of the causeway?
options: Nala
Hanuman
Sugriva
Vibhishana
questions.explain: The epic names an engineer and narrates the works at length — logistics treated as worth telling, immediately before the battle it is famous for.

questions.stem: What is the correct engineering order for building a causeway across a shoal?
options: Sound the depths, drop a rubble core, bind it, fill the voids, then surface it
Lay the surface slabs first, then build down to the seabed
Fill with sand, then add stone on top with no binding
Drive piles the full width, then pour the surface
questions.explain: You cannot surface a road before something is under it. Load spreading matters more than the size of individual stones.

questions.stem: What does Rama do with Lanka after the war?
options: Installs Vibhishana as king rather than annexing it
Annexes it to Kosala
Destroys the city completely
Leaves it without a ruler
questions.explain: The settlement is designed to show the war’s stated aim was honest: to right a specific wrong, not to take territory.

questions.stem: Kumbhakarna tells Ravana plainly that he is in the wrong — and then fights for him and dies. Why does the epic include him?
options: As a warning: honesty without the courage to act on it changes nothing
As comic relief
To show that family loyalty is always correct
To prove Ravana was blameless
questions.explain: He is set beside Vibhishana on purpose. Two people see the same wrong; the poem follows what each does about it, and judges accordingly.

questions.stem: Why does Valmiki give Ravana a formidable education — Vedic scholar, musician, astrologer?
options: So his fall is a tragedy about one ungoverned appetite, not a story about a stupid villain
To suggest that learning causes evil
Because Ravana wrote part of the epic
To pad out the narrative
questions.explain: An antagonist who is stupid teaches nothing. The poem builds him up carefully so the point lands.

questions.stem: What does the term dharmasankata describe?
options: A crisis where two genuine duties conflict and no option is clean
A formal legal court
A ritual of atonement
A military formation
questions.explain: Both epics are built around these. They dramatise the cost of each path rather than supplying a rule — which is why they still work as teaching texts.

questions.stem: What was characteristic of Indian Ocean hull construction for most of recorded history?
options: Planks sewn together with coir rope rather than nailed
Iron-riveted plates
Single hollowed logs only
Clinker-built with iron nails, as in northern Europe
questions.explain: A sewn hull flexes in a swell and can be repaired on a beach with no forge — a serious advantage on long monsoon routes.

questions.stem: The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea is useful to historians because it...
options: names Indian ports, goods and sailing seasons, letting us cross-check archaeology
is the oldest surviving Indian text
contains a map of the whole Indian Ocean
records the Ramayana in Greek
questions.explain: It is a first-century working handbook for merchants, which makes it unusually concrete about trade.

questions.stem: The Ramanathaswamy temple at Rameswaram illustrates which common pattern in Indian sacred architecture?
options: An old sacred association with much later standing structures, grown by accretion
A single building completed in one campaign
A structure built entirely in the twentieth century
A temple with no later additions at all
questions.explain: Dating "the temple" as one object is usually a mistake. Patrons kept adding halls, gateways and corridors over centuries.

questions.stem: In what order does the Lanka campaign actually proceed in the epic?
options: Alliance, reconnaissance, crossing, final embassy, then battle
Battle, then alliance, then crossing
Crossing, then reconnaissance, then alliance
Embassy, battle, then reconnaissance
questions.explain: Intelligence first, then diplomacy, then engineering, and only then fighting. The sequence is a comment in itself.

questions.stem: A geologist and a devotee disagree about Adam’s Bridge. What is the historian’s job here?
options: Keep the physical and the cultural claims in separate categories and assess each on its own evidence
Decide which one is lying
Declare the question unanswerable and drop it
Accept whichever is more popular
questions.explain: The shoal’s formation is a question for cores and surveys. The epic’s meaning is a question for literature and practice. Confusing the two serves neither.

questions.stem: Roughly how long is the Mahabharata?
options: About 100,000 shlokas — some ten times the Iliad and Odyssey combined
About 24,000 verses
About 700 verses
About 1,000 verses
questions.explain: 24,000 is the Ramayana; 700 is the Bhagavad Gita, which sits inside the Mahabharata.

questions.stem: What does the Mahabharata say about its own composition?
options: That it grew from a shorter work called Jaya, into Bharata, into Mahabharata
That it was written in a single night
That it was translated from Persian
That it has never changed since composition
questions.explain: The text is candid about being layered. That is normal for epic literature and it is a gift to historians.

questions.stem: Where does the Bhagavad Gita sit within the Mahabharata?
options: Inside the Bhishma Parva, on the eve of battle
At the very end, after the war
In a separate appendix
Before the dice game
questions.explain: Eighteen chapters, about 700 verses, beginning from Arjuna’s collapse between the two armies.

questions.stem: What is the Gita’s central ethical move?
options: Do the work that is yours to do, without grasping at its results
Avoid all action in order to avoid all consequence
Always obey a promise regardless of outcome
Pursue victory by any available means
questions.explain: "Yoga-sthah kuru karmani" — established in steadiness, perform your actions. Equanimity sharpens judgement; it does not switch it off.

questions.stem: Which is the common MISreading of nishkama karma?
options: "Do not care what happens"
"Choose carefully, then release the craving for a particular outcome"
"Action without hunger for its fruit"
"Equanimity improves judgement"
questions.explain: You still choose by duty and conscience. What you let go of is the fear and craving that distort the choosing — the surgeon operating for applause operates worse.

questions.stem: Arjuna proposes walking away from the battle. How does the text treat that option?
options: It takes it seriously, then argues that standing still is itself an act with consequences
It ignores the suggestion entirely
It accepts it and the war is called off
It treats it as the correct answer
questions.explain: Chapter 3 is explicit: you cannot escape action merely by refusing to move. There is no neutral square on that board.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the disciplines the Gita offers?
options: Artha yoga, the discipline of wealth
Karma yoga, the discipline of action
Jnana yoga, the discipline of knowledge
Bhakti yoga, the discipline of devotion
questions.explain: Karma, jnana, bhakti and dhyana (meditation). The text does not insist that everyone is a warrior — only that everyone has work.

questions.stem: Gandhi, Tilak and Ambedkar all read the Gita very differently. What does that tell you?
options: Commentary and disagreement are part of the tradition, not a failure of it
That the text has no fixed meaning and says nothing
That only one of them read it correctly
That the text is a modern forgery
questions.explain: It has been commented on continuously for a thousand years — Shankara, Ramanuja, Madhva, Abhinavagupta, and then the moderns. Gandhi read the battlefield as allegory; others read it literally.

questions.stem: How does the Gita reach the reader?
options: As Sanjaya reporting a conversation to the blind king Dhritarashtra
As a direct first-person account by Arjuna
As a letter written after the war
As an inscription found at Kurukshetra
questions.explain: The epic is obsessively layered in narrators. It keeps reminding you that you are receiving an account, which is a free lesson in reading sources.

questions.stem: How long does the war at Kurukshetra last?
options: Eighteen days
Eighteen months
Eighteen years
A single day
questions.explain: Eighteen recurs throughout: eighteen days, eighteen books, eighteen chapters of the Gita, eighteen armies.

questions.stem: What do almost all the war’s turning points have in common?
options: Each involves breaking an agreed rule of engagement
Each is won by a clever new weapon
Each happens at dawn
Each is decided by a single duel fought fairly
questions.explain: Fighting after sunset, surrounding a lone boy, striking a man who has laid down his weapons, a mace blow below the waist. The epic notes every violation and never grants a clean victory.

questions.stem: Why is Abhimanyu trapped inside the Chakravyuha?
options: He had learned how to enter the formation but not how to withdraw from it
He forgot his weapons
He was betrayed by his own charioteer
He entered deliberately to die
questions.explain: The epic’s sharpest comment on partial education — and the point at which the war stops being a war and becomes a vendetta.

questions.stem: What makes the Chakravyuha formation work defensively?
options: Its rotational symmetry — a gap anywhere lets an attacker cut across the layers
Its height advantage
The use of elephants only
Its reliance on archers positioned behind a river
questions.explain: Concentric rotating layers, easy to enter and designed to be impossible to leave. Symmetry is the whole mechanism.

questions.stem: In Drona’s famous test, what makes Arjuna’s answer the right one?
options: He reports seeing only the target — everything irrelevant has been excluded
He sees the whole tree and describes it in detail
He refuses to shoot at all
He asks for a better bow
questions.explain: Asked again, he says he sees only the bird’s eye. The lesson is about attention at the moment of action.

questions.stem: Why does the Ekalavya episode sit uncomfortably beside Drona’s test?
options: It shows talent being deliberately throttled by social gatekeeping, and the epic does not soften it
It proves Drona was the better archer
It shows that self-teaching never works
It is a later addition with no manuscript support
questions.explain: Refused instruction because of his birth, Ekalavya teaches himself and becomes better — and is made to give up his bow-thumb. Including that is the braver thing for a text to do.

questions.stem: Why is Karna’s chariot wheel sinking a plausible detail rather than just a plot device?
options: A light spoked chariot is fast on hard ground and useless on soft ground
Chariots had no wheels in this period
Chariots were made of stone
Chariots were only used for transport, never in battle
questions.explain: The epic praises the archer; the axle decides the battle. A chariot is a workshop someone decided to fight from.

questions.stem: What did excavation at Hastinapura actually establish?
options: A Painted Grey Ware settlement with evidence of flood damage
An inscription naming the Pandavas
The chariots used in the war
Nothing — the site has never been dug
questions.explain: Suggestive, since the epic also mentions a flood — but no archaeologist can confirm the war. What we can say is that the epic is set in a material culture that existed.

questions.stem: What is the honest position on dating the Mahabharata war?
options: It is unresolved; estimates range widely and most historians date only the material setting
It is firmly fixed at 3102 BCE by consensus
It has been dated precisely by radiocarbon
It is agreed to be entirely fictional with no setting
questions.explain: Traditional reckoning gives 3102 BCE; astronomical reconstructions range from the 31st to the 9th century BCE; academic historians place the setting around 1000 BCE and decline to date the events.

questions.stem: How does the Mahabharata handle the aftermath of the war?
options: It gives an entire book to the women of both sides mourning, and the victors inherit an empty country
It ends immediately with a victory celebration
It skips to a golden age with no mention of losses
It does not mention the aftermath at all
questions.explain: The Stri Parva is the answer to anyone who thinks this is a poem that glorifies war.

questions.stem: In what language are most of Ashoka’s edicts written?
options: Prakrit, the spoken language
Classical Sanskrit
Pali only
Persian
questions.explain: Written in Brahmi across most of the subcontinent, Kharosthi in the north-west, and Greek and Aramaic at Kandahar. An order nobody can read is decoration.

questions.stem: What makes Ashoka’s Major Rock Edict 13 unusual among ancient royal inscriptions?
options: It gives casualty figures and expresses the king’s remorse
It is written in verse
It lists the king’s ancestors for twenty generations
It threatens neighbouring kingdoms with invasion
questions.explain: Around 150,000 deported and 100,000 killed in Kalinga, with many more dead afterwards. No other ancient ruler published his regret.

questions.stem: What does Ashoka’s Rock Edict 12 instruct?
options: Do not praise your own sect while disparaging others
All subjects must become Buddhist
Brahmins are exempt from taxation
Temples must be built in every district
questions.explain: It adds that whoever reviles another’s faith out of devotion damages the very thing they are devoted to. Ashoka funded Buddhist, Brahmanical, Jain and Ajivika establishments alike.

questions.stem: What does dhamma mean in Ashoka’s edicts?
options: Conduct — respect for elders, decent treatment of servants, generosity to all sects, non-injury
A specific set of Buddhist doctrines all subjects must profess
The king’s absolute legal authority
A tax levied for religious institutions
questions.explain: He says he gave up the royal hunt, planted shade trees, dug wells, built rest-houses and appointed inspectors. Judge it by the wells.

questions.stem: Which scripts descend from Brahmi?
options: Devanagari, Tamil, Bengali, Telugu, Sinhala, Thai and Khmer among many others
Only Devanagari
Only the scripts of northern India
Arabic and Persian
questions.explain: Brahmi is the ancestor of nearly every script used in South and Southeast Asia today — one of the most consequential inventions in the region.

questions.stem: Brahmi is an abugida. What does that mean?
options: Each consonant carries an inherent vowel, changed by attached marks
Each sign stands for a whole word
It has no vowels at all
It is written right to left
questions.explain: That is why Indian scripts look dense and compact compared with an alphabet writing every vowel as a separate letter.

questions.stem: How did James Prinsep decipher Brahmi in 1837?
options: By comparing bilingual Indo-Greek coins giving the same king’s name in Greek and Brahmi
By finding a Brahmi-Sanskrit dictionary
By using a computer concordance
By asking surviving readers of the script
questions.explain: Once Brahmi could be read, Ashoka’s edicts became legible and the chronology of early India could be built. One decipherment reorganised a field.

questions.stem: Why is the ritual at a stupa to walk around it rather than enter it?
options: A stupa is solid — there is no interior to enter
Entry is reserved for monks
The interior floods seasonally
The entrance was lost in antiquity
questions.explain: The railing, gateways and circumambulation path exist to organise that walk. The architecture follows from the solidity.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order from the ground up?
options: Medhi, anda, harmika, yashti, chhatra
Anda, medhi, chhatra, yashti, harmika
Harmika, medhi, anda, yashti, chhatra
Yashti, chhatra, anda, medhi, harmika
questions.explain: Drum, dome, the square railed box on top, the mast, then the tiered parasols. The umbrella cannot float.

questions.stem: The famous carved gateways at Sanchi date from which period?
options: Satavahana, around the 1st century BCE — later than the Ashokan core
Ashokan, 3rd century BCE
Gupta, 5th century CE
Mughal, 17th century CE
questions.explain: The brick core is Ashokan; it was encased in stone in the 2nd century BCE and the toranas came later still. Monuments are usually several buildings.

questions.stem: How is the Buddha represented in Sanchi’s early carvings?
options: Only by symbols — a footprint, an empty seat, a wheel, a tree
As a standing figure in robes
As a seated figure under an umbrella
He is not referred to at all
questions.explain: Figural images appear later, at Mathura and Gandhara. The symbolic phase is a real art-historical stage, not a shortage of skill.

questions.stem: What do Sanchi’s hundreds of short donor inscriptions reveal?
options: Much of it was paid for by women, merchants and ordinary monks, not only kings
All funding came from the Mauryan treasury
The site was built by forced labour
The donors were all foreign
questions.explain: Individual railings and panels carry individual names. It is one of the best windows we have onto non-royal patronage in early India.

questions.stem: Which Ashokan sculpture became the state emblem of the Republic of India?
options: The lion capital from Sarnath
The bull capital from Rampurva
The Lauriya Nandangarh pillar
The Dhauli elephant
questions.explain: Adopted on 26 January 1950. The pillars are single shafts of Chunar sandstone with a famously smooth polish.

questions.stem: How should the Arthashastra be read?
options: As accumulated statecraft compiled over centuries, not a Mauryan policy document
As Chandragupta’s personal diary
As a religious text
As a nineteenth-century forgery
questions.explain: The surviving text reached its final form some centuries after the Mauryas. It is a manual of what works for a ruler — which is why reading it beside Ashoka’s edicts is so instructive.

questions.stem: What was the backbone of Mauryan state revenue?
options: Land revenue — a share of the harvest on surveyed land
Customs duties on sea trade
Tribute from foreign kings
Temple donations
questions.explain: Conventionally around one-sixth but variable, plus tolls, mint and mining royalties, irrigation cess and taxes on crafts.

questions.stem: Why must Megasthenes’ Indica be used carefully?
options: It survives only as quotations in later Greek writers
It was written a thousand years after the events
It is written in an undeciphered script
It was proven to be a forgery in 1890
questions.explain: We read him through other people’s selections. His description of Pataliputra’s timber walls does match the excavated palisade.

questions.stem: What did Nalanda teach besides Buddhist doctrine?
options: Logic and debate, grammar, medicine, metaphysics, mathematics and astronomy
Only scripture recitation
Only medicine
Military strategy exclusively
questions.explain: Students came from Tibet, China, Korea, Central Asia, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia, and admission involved an oral examination at the gate.

questions.stem: Whose travel account gives us one of the best descriptions of Nalanda?
options: Xuanzang, who studied there in the 630s
Megasthenes
Abdur Razzaq
Domingo Paes
questions.explain: Nalanda ran for roughly seven hundred years from the fifth century and was sacked around 1193 during the Ghurid campaigns in Bihar.

questions.stem: What is the main caution about calling the Gupta period a "golden age"?
options: The same period shows hardening caste restrictions and declining women’s property rights in the legal literature
There were no scientific achievements
The Guptas never existed
The period lasted only ten years
questions.explain: Gupta gold coinage is superb, and gold coinage is not a measure of how most people lived. Golden ages are usually golden for somebody in particular.

questions.stem: What holds the tower of the Brihadeeswarar temple together?
options: Nothing but weight and geometry — the granite blocks interlock, with no mortar
Lime mortar between every course
Iron cramps set in lead
A concrete core
questions.explain: A 66 m tower completed in 1010 CE, standing through earthquakes for over a thousand years. Interlocking cut stone, no mortar in the vimana.

questions.stem: How was the roughly 80-tonne capstone raised 66 m?
options: Up a very long earth ramp on timber rollers, later dug away
By a system of iron cranes
By flooding the site and floating it up
It was cast in place from molten stone
questions.explain: A shallow gradient over kilometres is easier than a steep one over hundreds of metres. Local tradition names a village, Sarapallam, as where the ramp began.

questions.stem: Dravida towers of this period are corbelled rather than arched. What does that require?
options: A very thick base, because load travels down through the mass
A lightweight timber frame
Flying buttresses
A keystone at the apex
questions.explain: Each course steps slightly inward and the stones must be dressed to fit precisely, because any gap concentrates stress.

questions.stem: How does the Thanjavur temple cope with soft alluvial soil?
options: A broad compacted platform spreads the load, rather than a deep foundation
Deep stone piles driven to bedrock
A floating raft of timber
It sits on natural granite bedrock at the surface
questions.explain: The same principle as a snowshoe. There is no deep foundation in the modern sense.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the lost-wax process?
options: Wax model, clay investment, burn out the wax, pour the bronze, break the mould, finish
Clay model, pour the bronze, add wax, polish
Pour the bronze, carve it, then coat in wax
Carve the bronze from a solid block, then wax it
questions.explain: The wax has to leave before the metal arrives. Madhuchchhishta vidhana — the lost beeswax method.

questions.stem: Why is every solid-cast Chola bronze unique?
options: The mould must be broken to release the casting
Each was signed by a different artist
Each used a different metal
The temple forbade copies
questions.explain: There is no reusable mould in this technique. Bronze casting continues today around Swamimalai using the same method.

questions.stem: Why do Chola bronzes have lugs and carefully balanced poses?
options: They are processional images, carried out of the temple on poles
They were designed to hang from ceilings
They were weighed for tax purposes
They were mounted on chariot wheels
questions.explain: The Nataraja balancing on one foot inside a ring of flame is theology and statics at the same time.

questions.stem: In the Uttaramerur system, how was a committee member finally selected?
options: By lot — palm-leaf tickets drawn from a pot by a boy who could not read
By a show of hands in the assembly
By the king’s appointment
By hereditary succession
questions.explain: Kudavolai, the pot-ticket. The boy could not read, so he could not favour anyone — and the whole assembly watched.

questions.stem: What is the most striking feature of the Uttaramerur disqualification rules?
options: Anyone who has not submitted his accounts — or whose relatives have not — is barred
Only men over seventy could serve
Candidates had to be unmarried
Only priests were eligible
questions.explain: Audit first, then eligibility, plus a three-year bar on repeat terms. The achievement is accountability and rotation, not universal suffrage.

questions.stem: Why is "ancient Indian democracy" an overstatement for Uttaramerur?
options: There were property and literacy qualifications, and the franchise was narrow
The inscriptions are forgeries
The assembly never actually met
The rules applied only to one year
questions.explain: The genuine achievement is rule-bound, auditable, rotating local government — written on a wall where anyone could check it.

questions.stem: What was the strategic target of Rajendra I’s naval expedition around 1025 CE?
options: The Strait of Malacca, the chokepoint for China trade
The Persian Gulf oil ports
The Red Sea route to Egypt
The Maldives fisheries
questions.explain: The ports taken are listed in the Thanjavur inscriptions, which is how we know the campaign happened at all. It was about leverage, not settlement.

questions.stem: How did the monsoon shape Indian Ocean voyages?
options: Winds reverse twice a year, so voyages had fixed seasons and crews wintered in foreign ports
Winds blow constantly from the west all year
There is no seasonal pattern
Ships could only sail at night
questions.explain: South-westerly roughly June to September, north-easterly November to February. Months spent in foreign ports is how scripts, religions and epics travelled.

questions.stem: Whose inscriptions turn up as far away as Sumatra, showing the reach of South Indian trade?
options: The Ayyavole and Manigramam merchant guilds
The Chola royal navy only
Portuguese trading companies
Buddhist monastic orders
questions.explain: The guilds traded across the Bay of Bengal and knew every harbour — which is also where a campaign got its intelligence.

questions.stem: What do Chola temple inscriptions tell us that most sources do not?
options: Exact allowances and wages for priests, accountants, musicians, dancers and watchmen
The personal letters of the kings
The texts of lost epics
The military casualty figures of every battle
questions.explain: A big temple is legible as an economic institution — employer, landowner, bank and granary — as much as a religious one.

questions.stem: What systematic bias do temple-wall inscriptions carry?
options: They record what donors wanted remembered, and are silent on famines, revolts and the poor
They systematically exaggerate rainfall
They were written centuries after the events
They are written in an undeciphered script
questions.explain: Dated and precise about grants; blind to everything a donor had no reason to carve. Knowing a source’s silences is half of using it.

questions.stem: Why does peninsular India rely on tanks rather than large river canals?
options: A seasonal monsoon and hard rock geology make storing rain more important than diverting rivers
There are no rivers at all
Canals were forbidden by law
The soil cannot hold water
questions.explain: Bunded tanks across shallow valleys, often chained so one overflows into the next. Inscriptions record desilting duties and penalties for neglect.

questions.stem: The Sun Temple at Konark is designed as what?
options: The sun god’s chariot, with twenty-four wheels and seven horses
A stepped pyramid
A fortified palace
A Buddhist stupa
questions.explain: Built under Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty around 1250 CE. European sailors called it the Black Pagoda and used it as a landmark.

questions.stem: How do Konark’s wheels function as sundials?
options: Eight major spokes divide the daylight into roughly three-hour parts, halved again by minor spokes
The wheels rotate once per day
Water poured into the hub drains at a fixed rate
The wheels cast no shadow and mark only noon
questions.explain: A rod at the axle throws a shadow across the rim. Beads along the rim subdivide further — and the symmetry is calibration, not decoration.

questions.stem: What is the state of Konark’s main tower today?
options: Collapsed, with causes debated; the porch survives and was filled in to stabilise it
Fully intact
Never built beyond the plinth
Dismantled and re-erected in Delhi
questions.explain: Structural failure, subsidence and later damage are all argued. A nineteenth-century intervention filled the jagamohana to stop it following the tower down.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the Kalinga (Odishan) rekha deul silhouette?
options: Walls rise nearly vertically, then turn in sharply near the top
A stepped pyramid of diminishing storeys
A bulbous onion dome
A flat roof with no tower
questions.explain: Compare Dravida in the south, where the tower is a stepped pyramid, and the gentler curve of Khajuraho. Odisha also preserves unusually rich builders’ manuals.

questions.stem: What did Aryabhata argue causes the apparent daily motion of the stars?
options: The Earth’s rotation on its own axis
The stars being carried on separate rotating spheres
The sun dragging them round
An optical illusion caused by the atmosphere
questions.explain: He used the image of a passenger in a moving boat seeing the bank slide past, and gave the sidereal day accurately as about 23 h 56 m 4 s.

questions.stem: How did Aryabhata explain eclipses?
options: As shadows: the Earth’s on the Moon, and the Moon’s on us
As a demon swallowing the Sun
As clouds of unusual density
As the Moon changing its own brightness
questions.explain: Because it is geometry, it can be computed in advance — and he gives methods for the size and duration of the shadow.

questions.stem: Aryabhata gives π as 3.1416 and attaches the word asanna. Why does that word matter?
options: It means "approximate" — he does not claim the value is exact
It means "sacred", marking the number as divine
It means "measured", claiming experimental proof
It is the name of his teacher
questions.explain: Labelling the limits of your own result is what distinguishes a scientific claim from a pronouncement.

questions.stem: Which text first sets out the arithmetic of zero and negative numbers?
options: Brahmagupta’s Brahmasphutasiddhanta, 628 CE
Aryabhata’s Aryabhatiya, 499 CE
Bhaskara II’s Lilavati, 1150 CE
The Bakhshali manuscript
questions.explain: He explains negatives as debts and fortunes, and notes that dividing by zero gives nothing usable.

questions.stem: Which gives a clear, securely dated decimal zero as a digit?
options: The Gwalior inscription of 876 CE
The Bakhshali manuscript, whose date is contested
Ashoka’s edicts
The Rigveda
questions.explain: From India the system passed through the Islamic world — al-Khwarizmi wrote about "Hindu reckoning" — and reached Europe with Fibonacci in 1202.

questions.stem: What did Madhava of Sangamagrama achieve around 1400 CE?
options: Infinite series for π, sine and cosine — calculus-adjacent results
The first telescope
A mechanical calculating machine
The decimal point
questions.explain: In Europe these results are associated with Newton, Leibniz, Gregory and Taylor two to three centuries later.

questions.stem: What makes Jyeshthadeva’s Yuktibhasha (c. 1530) remarkable?
options: It gives derivations rather than only results, and is written in Malayalam
It is the oldest Sanskrit mathematical text
It was commissioned by the Mughal court
It proves Fermat’s Last Theorem
questions.explain: Something close to proof, including an early treatment of what we would call term-by-term integration.

questions.stem: What does the Samrat Yantra at Jaipur measure, and how accurately?
options: Local solar time, to within a couple of seconds
Rainfall, to the nearest millimetre
Star brightness, in magnitudes
Latitude only, to the nearest degree
questions.explain: A roughly 27 m gnomon with curved quadrant scales. Bigger instruments resolve a shadow more finely — which is why it is built in stone.

questions.stem: Jai Singh II owned European telescopes and tables. Why did he still build huge masonry instruments?
options: A longer arc can be subdivided more finely, so size buys precision
He did not trust foreign instruments at all
Masonry was cheaper than brass
Telescopes were banned by the court
questions.explain: He had Euclid and Ptolemy translated and compared Indian, Islamic and European tables, publishing where they disagreed. That habit is the science.

questions.stem: How many observatories did Sawai Jai Singh II build?
options: Five — Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Mathura and Varanasi
One, at Jaipur
Two, at Delhi and Agra
Twelve, one per zodiac sign
questions.explain: The Jaipur one survives best, with about twenty instruments, and was inscribed by UNESCO in 2010.

questions.stem: What does the Ram Yantra measure?
options: Altitude and azimuth of a celestial body
Local time from a shadow
Ecliptic coordinates per zodiac sign
Declination and hour angle of a star
questions.explain: The Samrat Yantra gives time, the Rashivalaya ecliptic coordinates, and the Chakra Yantra declination and hour angle.

questions.stem: What working habits characterised the siddhanta tradition?
options: Compressed verse for memorisation, commentaries that corrected predecessors, and models checked against observation
Secrecy, with results never written down
Reliance on a single unchallenged authority
Rejection of all foreign astronomy
questions.explain: Brahmagupta attacked parts of Aryabhata’s system and some of those criticisms were right. That argument is the evidence it was a working science.

questions.stem: Vijayanagara was founded in 1336 CE by whom?
options: Harihara I and Bukka I of the Sangama line
Krishnadevaraya
Rajaraja Chola
Rana Kumbha
questions.explain: Krishnadevaraya is the best-remembered ruler but reigned much later, 1509–1529, and belonged to the Tuluva line.

questions.stem: Why is the landscape at Hampi full of enormous rounded granite boulders?
options: Exfoliation — the outer shells of ancient granite peel away over millions of years
They were carried there by glaciers
They were quarried and abandoned by Vijayanagara masons
They are the remains of a meteorite impact
questions.explain: Part of the Dharwar craton, some of the oldest exposed rock on Earth. The builders used the boulders rather than levelling them.

questions.stem: What is the famous Stone Chariot at Hampi, actually?
options: A shrine to Garuda, assembled from several granite blocks
A single monolithic block carved in place
A real chariot petrified by lightning
A Mughal-era folly
questions.explain: The joints are visible once you know to look, and its wheels once turned. It was never meant to move.

questions.stem: What are the "musical pillars" in the Vittala temple?
options: Structural columns whose slender colonettes ring at different pitches when struck
Hollow pipes with an internal water organ
Metal rods set into stone sockets
A nineteenth-century addition
questions.explain: The pitch depends on each colonette’s dimensions. Decades of visitors striking them with coins caused real damage, so access is now restricted.

questions.stem: What is unusual about Virupaksha temple among the Hampi monuments?
options: It is older than the empire and has never stopped being worshipped
It was built entirely after 1565
It is made of brick rather than granite
It was never finished
questions.explain: A shrine existed here before 1336 and it was enlarged under Krishnadevaraya. Continuity is itself a historical fact worth noticing.

questions.stem: What is the most durable legacy of Vijayanagara’s engineering?
options: Irrigation canals that still water the fields around Kamalapura
The city walls
The royal mint
The elephant stables
questions.explain: A diversion weir on the Tungabhadra fed gravity canals, some cut through solid rock. For a city famous for being destroyed, the plumbing outlasted everything.

questions.stem: What does the numbering on the blocks of Hampi’s stepped tank tell us?
options: It was cut elsewhere and assembled on site like a kit of parts
It records the names of donors
It is a calendar
It marks water levels through the year
questions.explain: The tank was excavated in the 1980s. Mason’s marks are one of the most direct kinds of evidence about how a building was actually organised.

questions.stem: What should you know about names like "Lotus Mahal" and "Queen’s Bath"?
options: They are modern labels invented by later visitors, and the functions are argued
They are the original Vijayanagara names, recorded in inscriptions
They were coined by Krishnadevaraya himself
They come from Persian chronicles of the 1440s
questions.explain: Nineteenth-century coinages. Archaeologists argue function from plan, position and inscription — and sometimes change their minds.

questions.stem: Why were imported warhorses so politically important in the Deccan?
options: The region cannot breed good cavalry mounts, so supply was a strategic lever
Horses were used as currency
Horses were sacred and could not be bred locally
Local horses were larger but slower
questions.explain: Climate, fodder and disease all work against it. When the Portuguese took Goa in 1510 they used horse-trade licensing as a diplomatic instrument with every Deccan power.

questions.stem: What was the gold coin of Vijayanagara that the Portuguese called the pagoda?
options: The varaha
The panam
The jital
The rupiya
questions.explain: Smaller panams and copper jitals handled everyday trade. Revenue came from land, gate customs, market dues and tribute.

questions.stem: Why were Vijayanagara’s bazaars built right in front of major temples?
options: Temples were economic institutions — landowners, employers and holders of endowments
To keep merchants under priestly surveillance
Because temple land was the only flat ground
To shelter traders from monsoon flooding
questions.explain: Long colonnaded streets with stone platforms and pillared shop fronts have been excavated in front of the temples.

questions.stem: Razzaq and Paes both describe Vijayanagara as enormous. What is the right way to use them?
options: Note their motives, then cross-check against inscriptions and archaeology
Accept the figures as precise census data
Dismiss them as pure invention
Use whichever gives the larger number
questions.explain: Razzaq reports to a court assessing a rival; Paes writes for people deciding whether to invest. Neither is lying, exactly. Both have reason to exaggerate.

questions.stem: Who defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565?
options: A coalition of the Deccan sultanates — Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda and Bidar
The Mughal empire under Akbar
The Portuguese at Goa
The Marathas under Shivaji
questions.explain: Rama Raya was killed, the army broke, and the capital was plundered. The dynasty itself continued from Penukonda and Chandragiri for decades.

questions.stem: What does the archaeology show about Vijayanagara after 1565?
options: Burning in some quarters, continuity in others, and worship at Virupaksha never stopping
Total, uniform destruction within weeks
No change at all until the nineteenth century
The site was immediately resettled as a Mughal garrison
questions.explain: The abandonment of the capital was real and it was a process. History usually runs slower than the story told about it afterwards.

questions.stem: The Taj Mahal was built for whom, and by whom?
options: For Mumtaz Mahal, by Shah Jahan
For Nur Jahan, by Jahangir
For Akbar, by Jahangir
For Jodha Bai, by Akbar
questions.explain: Mumtaz died in 1631 at Burhanpur; building ran roughly 1632–1653. The chief architect is generally credited as Ustad Ahmad Lahauri.

questions.stem: Where did the Taj’s white marble come from?
options: Makrana in Rajasthan, about 400 km away
Carrara in Italy
Local quarries beside the Yamuna
The Hindu Kush
questions.explain: Makrana marble does not yellow and glows at dusk, which is why it was worth hauling that far.

questions.stem: What problem does a double dome solve?
options: A dome tall enough for the skyline would feel oppressive inside, and vice versa
It halves the amount of marble needed
It prevents rainwater pooling
It allows a staircase inside the dome
questions.explain: An inner shell proportioned to the chamber, an outer shell proportioned to the silhouette, and a void between. You never see both at once.

questions.stem: Why do the Taj’s minarets lean very slightly outward?
options: So that if they ever failed they would fall away from the tomb
To correct an error in the foundations
To improve the acoustics of the courtyard
They have subsided over time and were built vertical
questions.explain: A deliberate engineering decision, like the foundations of timber and rubble kept permanently wet beside the Yamuna.

questions.stem: Why do the letters in the Taj’s calligraphic panels grow taller as they rise?
options: So they appear a uniform size when read from the ground
Because the calligrapher ran out of space
To mark the most important verses
To match the taper of the dome
questions.explain: Amanat Khan signed his work on the building — either confidence or impertinence, and probably both.

questions.stem: What single element breaks the Taj’s otherwise perfect bilateral symmetry?
options: Shah Jahan’s cenotaph, added later off the central axis
One of the four minarets
The main gateway
The western mosque
questions.explain: Mumtaz’s cenotaph sits on the axis; his does not. The asymmetry is the one thing that tells you the building outlived its plan.

questions.stem: What is parchin kari?
options: Stone inlay — semi-precious stones cut and fitted into recesses in marble
Painting on wet plaster
Carving marble in relief
Gilding with beaten gold leaf
questions.explain: Known in Europe as pietra dura. A single flower spray can contain dozens of pieces, fitted so the joints are invisible to a fingertip.

questions.stem: What is a charbagh?
options: A square garden quartered by raised walkways carrying water channels
A circular garden around a central tomb
A terraced hillside garden
A walled orchard with no formal plan
questions.explain: Each quadrant is often quartered again, so the pattern repeats at smaller scale. It is irrigation as much as symbolism.

questions.stem: Which building is the Taj Mahal’s direct architectural ancestor?
options: Humayun’s Tomb in Delhi
The Qutb Minar
Fatehpur Sikri’s Buland Darwaza
The Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur
questions.explain: Completed around 1570 and commissioned by Empress Bega Begum — the first great garden tomb in India.

questions.stem: A red sandstone building with flat lintels on brackets and chhatris most likely dates from which reign?
options: Akbar’s
Shah Jahan’s
Aurangzeb’s
Bahadur Shah Zafar’s
questions.explain: White marble, cusped arches, bulbous domes and pietra dura point to Shah Jahan. You can almost date these buildings by material and opening.

questions.stem: Which best describes Mughal architecture?
options: A synthesis: Central Asian arches and domes with Indian brackets, chhatris and craft labour
A pure import, built entirely by Persian craftsmen
Purely indigenous, with no outside influence
A direct copy of Ottoman mosque design
questions.explain: Fatehpur Sikri is the clearest single place to see the two traditions being argued out in stone.

questions.stem: Why is Fatehpur Sikri so well preserved?
options: It was abandoned within about fifteen years, so nobody kept rebuilding it
It was continuously restored by every later emperor
It was buried by sand until 1900
It was rebuilt in concrete in the 1950s
questions.explain: Water supply is the usual explanation for the abandonment, though political and strategic reasons are also argued.

questions.stem: What does sulh-i-kul mean as Akbar used it?
options: Peace with all — the state takes no side and no one may revile another’s faith
All religions are secretly the same
Islam is the only permitted religion of state
Religion is banned from public life
questions.explain: He abolished the pilgrimage tax and the jizya, and appointed Hindus including Todar Mal and Man Singh to the highest offices.

questions.stem: What does Aurangzeb’s reimposition of the jizya in 1679 illustrate?
options: A tolerance resting on one ruler’s character is reversible by the next
That Akbar’s policy had never existed
That the jizya was popular with all subjects
That Mughal policy never changed
questions.explain: The limits matter as much as the achievement. This was court policy, not a constitutional settlement.

questions.stem: What is the Razmnama?
options: A Persian translation of the Mahabharata made under Akbar
Akbar’s own memoir
A manual of Mughal artillery
A revenue survey of Bengal
questions.explain: Akbar’s maktab khana also translated the Ramayana, the Atharva Veda, the Yoga Vasistha, the Panchatantra and Bhaskara’s Lilavati. Badauni, who thought Akbar a heretic, worked on it.

questions.stem: The story that the Taj’s workers had their hands cut off afterwards is...
options: Unsupported by any contemporary evidence and rejected by historians
Recorded in the Ain-i-Akbari
Confirmed by Shah Jahan’s own farman
Supported by skeletal evidence from Taj Ganj
questions.explain: A workforce of roughly twenty thousand over two decades, some named in surviving ledgers, lived in the settlement still called Taj Ganj. Famous buildings attract invented stories.

questions.stem: Why is the gateway of an Indian hill fort usually set at a right angle inside a passage?
options: So nothing — elephant or ram — can build momentum against the doors
To shelter the gate from monsoon rain
To make the fort look larger
To allow carts to turn around inside
questions.explain: Combined with bastions that shoot along the wall rather than out from it, and a long exposed approach climb.

questions.stem: Why do bastions project out from a fort wall?
options: So defenders can shoot along the face of the wall, covering the ground attackers must cross
To add storage space
To hold heavier roofs
To make the wall taller
questions.explain: Flanking fire is the whole idea. A flat wall leaves a blind strip at its base exactly where an attacker wants to be.

questions.stem: What usually decides a hill-fort siege?
options: Water storage
The height of the walls
The number of gates
The quality of the stone
questions.explain: Rock-cut cisterns sized for a year or more. Walls can be repaired under fire; a dry cistern cannot be refilled in June.

questions.stem: Which is the largest fort in India?
options: Chittorgarh
Raigad
Golconda
Gwalior
questions.explain: About 280 hectares on a plateau. Kumbhalgarh, also in Mewar, has one of the longest perimeter walls in the world at around 36 km.

questions.stem: Who built the Vijaya Stambha at Chittorgarh, and what else does it record?
options: Rana Kumbha — and inscriptions inside list the rulers of his house
Maharana Pratap — and it records the battle of Haldighati
Akbar — and it records the 1568 siege
Shivaji — and it records the Ashta Pradhan
questions.explain: Nine storeys, around 37 m, raised in 1448 to commemorate a victory over the Sultan of Malwa.

questions.stem: What is the most defensible summary of Haldighati in 1576?
options: Tactically inconclusive; Pratap escaped and then recovered most of Mewar from the hills
A decisive Mughal victory that ended Mewar’s resistance
A decisive Rajput victory that expelled the Mughals from Rajasthan
A battle that never took place
questions.explain: Rajput bardic sources remember a heroic stand, Mughal chronicles a victory. Reading both is the honest approach — and the long campaign that followed matters more than the day.

questions.stem: What is ganimi kava?
options: A doctrine of mobility: strike supply lines, use the ghats and the monsoon, never give a set-piece battle
A system of land revenue
A naval signalling code
A style of fort construction
questions.explain: It is not a substitute for organisation but a product of it: intelligence, a fort network, and infantry drawn from the Mawal valleys.

questions.stem: How did the monsoon favour the Marathas in the Western Ghats?
options: Heavy cavalry and artillery bog down from June to September while light infantry still walks
It flooded the plains, forcing enemies into the hills
It made the sea routes safer for Maratha ships
It provided cover of fog for night attacks year-round
questions.explain: Terrain and season were the general. Local men knowing every goat track is not a tactic — it is a home.

questions.stem: Why did Shivaji build sea forts and a fleet?
options: Because the Siddis, Portuguese and English could land anywhere on an undefended coast
To trade directly with China
To transport his army faster than by land
Because the Mughals had no land army nearby
questions.explain: Sindhudurg and Vijaydurg sit on offshore rock. A kingdom with a coast and no fleet has a door with no latch.

questions.stem: Who, as Sarkhel, held the Konkan coast against European squadrons for three decades?
options: Kanhoji Angre
Tanaji Malusare
Baji Prabhu Deshpande
Sadashivrao Bhau
questions.explain: Roughly 1698–1729, against Portuguese, Dutch and English forces. Indian naval history is badly under-taught and this is the clearest case of it.

questions.stem: What was the Ashta Pradhan?
options: Shivaji’s council of eight ministers, from Peshwa to Panditrao
A tax of one-eighth on all produce
An eight-fort defensive line
A code of eight rules for soldiers
questions.explain: Intended as offices rather than hereditary gifts. Within two generations the Peshwa’s post had become hereditary and the real power — institutions drift.

questions.stem: How were chauth and sardeshmukhi collected?
options: As assessed shares against land measurement, with written receipts
By seizing whatever an army could carry
As a fixed annual tribute paid in horses
Only from merchants, never from land
questions.explain: Shivaji’s standing orders forbid touching the standing crop, the cattle or the women of a village. A soldier who burns a village destroys next year’s revenue — that is arithmetic, not mercy.

questions.stem: What change did Shivaji make to official record-keeping?
options: Court records were kept in Marathi and Sanskrit rather than Persian
Records were abolished to prevent espionage
All records were kept in Portuguese for trade
Records were kept only orally
questions.explain: A deliberate statement about whose state it was, and a practical one about who could read it.

questions.stem: Ahilyabai Holkar is chiefly remembered for what?
options: Public works — ghats, wells, roads, rest-houses and temples across India
Conquering Bengal
Founding the Maratha navy
Writing a treatise on statecraft
questions.explain: She ruled Malwa from Maheshwar for nearly thirty years and rebuilt the Kashi Vishwanath temple in 1780. Battles are remembered; wells are used.

questions.stem: What best explains the Maratha defeat at Panipat in 1761?
options: Supply lines cut a thousand kilometres from base, absent allies, and better enemy artillery
A sudden change of weather on the day
Superior numbers on the Afghan side alone
The death of the Peshwa during the battle
questions.explain: The Rajputs, Jats and Awadh were largely absent or hostile, partly because of how chauth had been collected from them. Logistics and diplomacy lost it before the fighting started.

questions.stem: What finally ended the hill-fort system that cavalry had never beaten?
options: Sustained siege artillery and company finance, by 1818
A series of earthquakes
The silting of the Konkan harbours
A treaty banning fortification
questions.explain: Both the Rajput and Maratha fort traditions lost to logistics and heavy guns, not to any failure of courage.
